items.stem: Which of the following specimens is acceptable for anaerobic bacterial culture?
options: Voided midstream urine in a sterile cup
Expectorated sputum from a pneumonia patient
Needle aspirate from a deep abscess, sent anaerobically
Surface swab of a chronic leg ulcer
items.why: Anaerobes are abundant in the normal flora of mucous membranes and skin, so any specimen that passes over these surfaces will grow anaerobes that have no clinical meaning. **Aspirates or tissue taken from a normally sterile site and protected from oxygen** are the preferred specimens.

whyNot.0: Voided urine passes through the distal urethra, which carries anaerobic normal flora; only suprapubic aspirates are suitable for anaerobic urine culture.
whyNot.1: Expectorated sputum is contaminated by the oral flora, which is rich in anaerobes, so a positive anaerobic culture cannot be interpreted.
whyNot.3: A surface swab of an ulcer picks up colonizing skin and environmental flora, and swabs also expose the specimen to air; deep tissue or an aspirate is preferred.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., anaerobes chapter (specimen selection and collection); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., anaerobic bacteriology chapter

items.stem: A cerebrospinal fluid specimen for bacterial culture is received from a patient with suspected acute meningitis, but it cannot be plated right away. How should the specimen be held until it is processed?
options: Mixed with sodium polyanethol sulfonate (SPS) to keep white cells from clumping
Kept at room temperature or 35–37 °C, never refrigerated
items.why: Common causes of bacterial meningitis, especially Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae, are fragile and lose viability in the cold. **CSF for bacterial culture is kept at room temperature or 35–37 °C and processed as soon as possible.** (CSF for viral studies is the exception and may be refrigerated.)

whyNot.0: Refrigeration is appropriate for many other specimens, but it can kill cold-sensitive meningitis pathogens such as N. meningitidis and H. influenzae.
whyNot.1: Freezing at −20 °C destroys bacterial viability and is never used to hold a CSF specimen for routine bacterial culture.
whyNot.2: SPS is the anticoagulant in blood culture bottles, not a CSF additive, and it actually inhibits some Neisseria species.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., specimen collection and processing chapter and CNS infections chapter

items.stem: Modified Thayer-Martin agar for the isolation of Neisseria gonorrhoeae contains several antimicrobial agents. Which agent is included mainly to inhibit swarming Proteus species?
items.why: Each additive in modified Thayer-Martin agar suppresses a different group of normal flora. **Trimethoprim lactate is added to suppress swarming Proteus**, which is intrinsically resistant to colistin and would otherwise overgrow the plate.

whyNot.0: Vancomycin suppresses gram-positive bacteria; it has no activity against gram-negative Proteus.
whyNot.2: Colistin inhibits most gram-negative bacilli, but Proteus species are intrinsically resistant to polymyxins such as colistin, which is why another agent is needed.
whyNot.3: Nystatin is an antifungal included to suppress yeasts such as Candida; it does not act on bacteria.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Neisseria chapter and culture media chapter

items.stem: A wound isolate is a catalase-positive, gram-positive coccus that occurs in clusters. Which test best separates Staphylococcus aureus from most coagulase-negative staphylococci?
items.why: S. aureus produces bound coagulase (clumping factor, detected by the slide test) and free coagulase (detected by the tube test), whereas most other staphylococci do not. **A positive coagulase test is the classic marker that separates S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci.**

whyNot.1: All staphylococci are catalase-positive, so this test separates staphylococci from streptococci but not S. aureus from other staphylococci.
whyNot.2: Novobiocin resistance is used among coagulase-negative staphylococci to recognize S. saprophyticus, not to identify S. aureus.
whyNot.3: The modified oxidase test separates Micrococcus (positive) from Staphylococcus (negative); S. aureus and the coagulase-negative staphylococci are both negative.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Staphylococcus chapter

items.stem: Sputum culture yields alpha-hemolytic, catalase-negative, gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. Which pair of results supports Streptococcus pneumoniae rather than a viridans streptococcus?
options: CAMP positive and hippurate hydrolysis positive
items.why: S. pneumoniae and the viridans streptococci are both alpha-hemolytic, so the key tests target pneumococcal traits. **S. pneumoniae is susceptible to optochin and is lysed by bile salts (bile soluble)**, while viridans streptococci are optochin resistant and bile insoluble.

whyNot.0: This is the expected pattern for viridans streptococci, the main organisms that must be ruled out.
whyNot.1: Bacitracin susceptibility and a positive PYR test point to Streptococcus pyogenes (group A), which is beta-hemolytic.
whyNot.3: CAMP and hippurate positivity characterize Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), which is usually beta-hemolytic.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Streptococcus and Enterococcus chapter

items.stem: A non-lactose-fermenting stool isolate gives K/A with gas and H2S on TSI. It is motile, indole negative, urease negative, and lysine decarboxylase positive. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Non-typhoidal Salmonella typically ferments glucose only (K/A), produces gas and abundant H2S, is motile, and is indole and urease negative. **A positive lysine decarboxylase helps separate Salmonella from Citrobacter**, another H2S-positive organism.

whyNot.0: Shigella is nonmotile and does not produce H2S, so it gives K/A without blackening; S. sonnei is also lysine decarboxylase negative.
whyNot.1: Proteus mirabilis can give K/A with H2S, but it is strongly urease positive, swarms on blood agar, and is lysine decarboxylase negative.
whyNot.2: E. coli usually ferments lactose (A/A with gas), is indole positive, and does not produce H2S.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: A burn-wound isolate is a non-lactose fermenter on MacConkey agar, oxidase positive, produces a diffusible blue-green pigment with a grape-like odor, and grows at 42 °C. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: P. aeruginosa is a nonfermenter that is oxidase positive and grows at 42 °C. **The blue-green color comes from pyocyanin, a pigment produced only by P. aeruginosa**, and its fruity, grape-like odor is a well-known clue.

whyNot.0: Acinetobacter is oxidase negative, appears as coccobacilli, and does not produce a blue-green pigment.
whyNot.2: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is usually oxidase negative and does not produce pyocyanin.
whyNot.3: Klebsiella pneumoniae ferments lactose (pink, often mucoid colonies on MacConkey) and is oxidase negative.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Pseudomonas, Burkholderia and similar organisms chapter

items.stem: Oxidase-positive, gram-negative diplococci from a urethral discharge grow on modified Thayer-Martin agar. In carbohydrate utilization tests, glucose is positive while maltose, lactose, and sucrose are negative. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Pathogenic Neisseria are separated by which sugars they degrade. **N. gonorrhoeae uses glucose only**, which fits both the pattern and the urethral source.

whyNot.0: N. meningitidis uses both glucose and maltose.
whyNot.1: N. lactamica uses glucose, maltose, and lactose; lactose use is its distinguishing feature.
whyNot.2: Moraxella catarrhalis is asaccharolytic (all sugars negative) and is recognized by positive DNase and butyrate esterase tests.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Neisseria and Moraxella chapter

items.stem: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is isolated from a throat swab. Which laboratory test determines whether this strain actually produces diphtheria toxin?
options: Brown halo around colonies on Tinsdale agar
items.why: Only strains carrying the tox gene (on a lysogenic beta-phage) produce diphtheria toxin, so species identification alone is not enough. **The Elek test shows toxin production as precipitin lines where toxin meets antitoxin in agar.** PCR for the tox gene is a rapid alternative, but it detects the gene rather than toxin expression.

whyNot.0: The Schick test is an intradermal skin test on a person to assess immunity to diphtheria toxin; it does not test the isolate.
whyNot.1: The Nagler reaction detects the lecithinase (alpha toxin) of Clostridium perfringens on egg-yolk agar, not diphtheria toxin.
whyNot.2: The brown halo reflects cystinase activity and supports species identification, but toxigenic and nontoxigenic strains both produce it.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., aerobic gram-positive bacilli chapter (Corynebacterium)

items.stem: During a flood season, rice-water stool is cultured. On TCBS agar the isolate forms flat yellow colonies; it is an oxidase-positive, curved gram-negative rod with a positive string test. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: V. cholerae causes profuse rice-water diarrhea and grows well on TCBS. **Yellow colonies on TCBS reflect sucrose fermentation**, and the string test (a mucoid string formed in 0.5% sodium deoxycholate) supports the genus Vibrio.

whyNot.1: V. parahaemolyticus does not ferment sucrose, so its colonies are green on TCBS; it is usually linked to raw seafood.
whyNot.2: Aeromonas grows poorly or not at all on TCBS and is string-test negative.
whyNot.3: Campylobacter is a microaerophile grown at 42 °C on selective Campylobacter media; it does not grow on TCBS.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Vibrio, Aeromonas and Campylobacter chapters

items.stem: An anaerobe from a gas gangrene wound is a large, boxcar-shaped gram-positive bacillus in which spores are rarely seen. On anaerobic blood agar, colonies show an inner zone of complete hemolysis surrounded by an outer zone of partial hemolysis. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: C. perfringens is the main cause of gas gangrene and typically shows few or no spores in clinical material. **The double zone of hemolysis on blood agar is characteristic of C. perfringens**; its lecithinase (alpha toxin) can be confirmed on egg-yolk agar with the Nagler reaction.

whyNot.0: C. tetani has round terminal spores (drumstick shape), tends to swarm, and causes tetanus rather than gas gangrene.
whyNot.1: C. difficile has oval subterminal spores, forms yellow ground-glass colonies on CCFA, and causes antibiotic-associated colitis.
whyNot.3: Bacillus cereus grows aerobically, is motile, and shows a single wide zone of beta-hemolysis; it is not an obligate anaerobe.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., anaerobes chapter (Clostridium)

items.stem: After 3 weeks on Löwenstein-Jensen medium, an isolate forms rough, buff, nonpigmented colonies. It is niacin positive, nitrate reduction positive, and catalase negative after heating to 68 °C. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: M. tuberculosis grows slowly as rough, buff, nonpigmented colonies. **It accumulates niacin and reduces nitrate**, and its catalase is heat-labile, so it is negative after heating to 68 °C.

whyNot.0: M. bovis is niacin negative and nitrate negative and is susceptible to thiophene-2-carboxylic acid hydrazide (TCH).
whyNot.2: M. kansasii is a photochromogen (turns yellow after light exposure), is niacin negative, and has strong heat-stable catalase.
whyNot.3: M. avium complex is niacin negative and nitrate negative and usually has heat-stable catalase.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Mycobacteria chapter

items.stem: A gram-negative coccobacillus from the CSF of an unvaccinated child grows on a medium without blood only in the zone between an X-factor disk and a V-factor disk. On horse blood agar it is nonhemolytic. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Haemophilus species are identified by their need for X factor (hemin) and V factor (NAD) and by hemolysis on horse or rabbit blood. **H. influenzae requires both X and V factors and is nonhemolytic**, which matches this isolate and its source.

whyNot.0: H. parainfluenzae requires V factor only, so it would also grow around the V disk alone.
whyNot.1: H. haemolyticus also requires both X and V factors, but it is beta-hemolytic on horse or rabbit blood agar.
whyNot.2: H. ducreyi requires X factor only and causes chancroid, a genital ulcer disease, not meningitis.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Haemophilus chapter

items.stem: Which test is used to verify that milk has been adequately pasteurized?
items.why: Alkaline phosphatase occurs naturally in raw milk and is inactivated at a temperature slightly above that needed to kill the heat-resistant pathogens targeted by pasteurization. **Residual alkaline phosphatase activity means pasteurization was inadequate or raw milk was mixed in.**

whyNot.0: The methylene blue reduction test estimates the bacterial load and keeping quality of raw milk; it does not check heat treatment.
whyNot.1: The standard plate count measures overall bacterial numbers; a low count does not prove that the correct time and temperature were reached.
whyNot.3: Coliforms in pasteurized milk mainly point to contamination after pasteurization, not to whether the heat treatment itself was adequate.

items.ref: Standard Methods for the Examination of Dairy Products (APHA), phosphatase test; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., food and water microbiology section

items.stem: A yeast from a vaginal swab is incubated in serum at 35–37 °C for 2–3 hours and produces short hyphal outgrowths with no constriction where they join the cell. Which organism is most likely?
items.why: The germ tube test is a rapid presumptive test for C. albicans. **True germ tubes have parallel walls with no constriction at the point of origin.** C. dubliniensis is also germ-tube positive, which should be kept in mind.

whyNot.0: C. glabrata forms small budding yeast cells only and produces neither germ tubes nor pseudohyphae.
whyNot.1: C. tropicalis may form pseudohyphal outgrowths that are constricted where they join the cell, a common false-positive reading.
whyNot.3: Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated, urease-positive yeast that does not form germ tubes.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Mycology chapter (yeasts)

items.stem: A nasopharyngeal swab in viral transport medium is collected for virus isolation and will reach the virology laboratory in about 24 hours. How should it be held during this time?
items.why: Most viruses lose infectivity quickly when warm, so specimens for culture are kept cold. **Refrigeration at 2–8 °C is recommended for short delays.** If storage must last beyond about 2–3 days, the specimen is frozen at −70 °C or lower.

whyNot.1: Freezing at −20 °C, especially with freeze-thaw cycles, damages many viruses and reduces recovery; −70 °C is used when freezing is needed.
whyNot.2: At room temperature, labile viruses lose infectivity and any contaminating bacteria can multiply.
whyNot.3: Incubator temperatures speed up the loss of viral infectivity; warm holding is used for some bacterial specimens, not viral ones.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Virology chapter (specimen collection, transport and storage)

items.stem: A patient has had fever for 2 days and dengue is suspected. Which test is most likely to detect the infection at this stage?
options: Hemagglutination inhibition on a single serum sample
items.why: In the first days of illness, dengue is detected by finding the virus or its products rather than antibodies. **NS1 antigen is detectable from the first day of fever and is most reliably found in about the first 5 days**; viral RNA can also be detected by RT-PCR in this window.

whyNot.0: IgM usually becomes detectable only around day 4–5 of illness, so it is often negative on day 2.
whyNot.1: IgG appears late in a primary infection, and a positive IgG on one sample may only reflect a past infection.
whyNot.2: Hemagglutination inhibition needs paired acute and convalescent sera to show a rise in titer; one early sample cannot confirm current infection.

items.ref: WHO, Dengue: Guidelines for Diagnosis, Treatment, Prevention and Control (2009), laboratory diagnosis chapter; CDC Dengue clinical testing guidance

items.stem: In a standard PCR cycle, what happens during the step performed at about 72 °C?
options: Double-stranded DNA separates into single strands
Primers bind to their complementary target sequences
A thermostable DNA polymerase extends the primers
Reverse transcriptase converts RNA into cDNA
items.why: Each PCR cycle has three steps: denaturation (about 94–95 °C), annealing (about 50–65 °C, depending on the primers), and extension. **At about 72 °C, Taq or another thermostable polymerase adds nucleotides to the primers**, copying the target.

whyNot.0: Strand separation is denaturation, which needs about 94–95 °C.
whyNot.1: Primer binding is annealing, done at a lower temperature (about 50–65 °C) set by the primers' melting temperatures.
whyNot.3: Reverse transcription is a separate step before cycling in RT-PCR, usually at about 42–50 °C; it is not part of each PCR cycle.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., molecular diagnostics chapter

items.stem: In a traditional anaerobic jar that uses a hydrogen- and CO2-generating envelope, what is the function of the palladium catalyst?
options: It generates carbon dioxide for organisms that need it
It combines hydrogen with residual oxygen to form water
It changes color to show that anaerobic conditions were reached
It absorbs the moisture that builds up inside the jar
items.why: The envelope releases hydrogen and CO2 when water is added. **The palladium catalyst joins hydrogen with the oxygen left in the jar to form water**, which is why droplets form on the jar walls. The catalyst is inactivated by moisture and H2S and must be reactivated by heating or replaced.

whyNot.0: CO2 comes from the generator envelope (for example, from sodium bicarbonate and citric acid), not from the catalyst.
whyNot.2: Anaerobiosis is shown by a separate indicator strip, such as methylene blue (turns colorless) or resazurin.
whyNot.3: The catalyst makes water rather than absorbing it; moisture is a by-product of its reaction.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., anaerobes chapter (anaerobic culture systems)

items.stem: Which organism's spores are used as the biological indicator to monitor a steam autoclave?
options: Bacillus atrophaeus (formerly Bacillus subtilis var. niger)
items.why: A biological indicator uses spores that are very resistant to the specific sterilizing agent. **Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores are highly resistant to moist heat**, so killing them shows that the autoclave cycle (typically 121 °C at 15 psi for at least 15 minutes) was effective.

whyNot.0: B. atrophaeus spores are the indicator for dry-heat and ethylene oxide sterilization.
whyNot.1: B. pumilus spores have been used to monitor ionizing (gamma) radiation sterilization.
whyNot.2: E. coli ATCC 25922 is a quality-control strain for susceptibility testing; as a non-spore-former it is killed far too easily to challenge an autoclave.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., control of microorganisms chapter (sterilization monitoring)

items.stem: When the quality-control strain Escherichia coli ATCC 25922 is tested by disk diffusion, the zone diameters for every antimicrobial are larger than the acceptable ranges. Which error is the most likely cause?
options: The agar was poured to a depth of 6 mm
The inoculum was lighter than the 0.5 McFarland standard
The antimicrobial disks lost potency through improper storage
The inoculum was heavier than the 0.5 McFarland standard
items.why: Disk diffusion is standardized with a 0.5 McFarland inoculum (about 1.5 × 10^8 CFU/mL) on Mueller-Hinton agar about 4 mm deep. **When zones are too large for all drugs, suspect an inoculum that is too light** (or agar that is too thin), because fewer bacteria let the drug diffuse farther before growth is visible.

whyNot.0: Agar that is too deep dilutes the drug in a larger volume, which gives smaller zones, not larger ones.
whyNot.2: Disks that have lost potency release less drug and give smaller zones.
whyNot.3: A heavy inoculum produces confluent growth sooner and gives smaller zones.

items.ref: CLSI M02 (Performance Standards for Antimicrobial Disk Susceptibility Tests); Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., antimicrobial susceptibility testing chapter

items.stem: Which type of cabinet has an open front with inward airflow and a HEPA-filtered vertical downflow over the work surface, protecting the worker, the specimen, and the environment?
items.why: Biological safety cabinets differ in which of the worker, the product, and the environment they protect. **A Class II cabinet combines an inward air curtain at the open front with HEPA-filtered downflow and exhaust**, protecting all three, and it is the type most used in clinical microbiology.

whyNot.0: A Class I cabinet draws unfiltered room air across the work surface, so it protects the worker and environment but not the specimen.
whyNot.1: A Class III cabinet is a gas-tight enclosure worked through attached gloves; it has no open front.
whyNot.2: A horizontal clean bench blows filtered air toward the operator, protecting only the product; it must never be used for infectious material.

items.ref: CDC/NIH, Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL), 6th ed., Appendix A; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., laboratory safety chapter

items.stem: A farmer from Ilocos has months of watery diarrhea, abdominal gurgling, weight loss, and low serum albumin. His stool contains larvae, adult worms, and peanut-shaped eggs about 36–45 µm long with a striated shell and flattened, inconspicuous polar plugs. How was this infection most likely acquired?
options: Swallowing embryonated eggs from soil-contaminated hands or food
Eating raw or undercooked small freshwater or brackish-water fish
Skin contact with soil containing filariform larvae
items.why: This is intestinal capillariasis due to Capillaria philippinensis (also called Paracapillaria philippinensis), first recognized in Northern Luzon. **Humans are infected by eating raw or undercooked small fish that carry the larvae**, and autoinfection explains the heavy worm burden and protein-losing enteropathy.

whyNot.0: Ingestion of embryonated eggs from soil is the route for Ascaris and Trichuris, not Capillaria philippinensis.
whyNot.2: Raw freshwater crabs transmit Paragonimus westermani, a lung fluke.
whyNot.3: Skin penetration by filariform larvae from soil is the route for hookworms and Strongyloides stercoralis.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Capillaria philippinensis chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Intestinal Capillariasis

items.stem: A fresh stool wet mount shows a larva about 250 µm long with a short buccal canal and a prominent genital primordium. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Strongyloides eggs hatch in the intestine, so rhabditiform larvae, not eggs, are the usual stage found in fresh stool. **A short buccal canal and a prominent genital primordium identify the S. stercoralis rhabditiform larva.**

whyNot.0: Hookworm rhabditiform larvae have a long buccal canal and a small genital primordium, and they appear only if stool stands long enough for the eggs to hatch.
whyNot.2: The S. stercoralis filariform larva has a notched tail and an esophagus about half its body length; it is not the stage usually seen in fresh stool except in hyperinfection.
whyNot.3: Hookworm filariform larvae develop in soil, have a pointed tail and a sheath, and are not expected in a fresh stool specimen.

items.ref: CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Strongyloidiasis and Hookworm; Garcia, Diagnostic Medical Parasitology, 6th ed., intestinal nematodes chapter

items.stem: Schistosomiasis japonica is endemic in several Philippine provinces, including areas of Leyte, Samar, and Mindanao. Which snail serves as the intermediate host of Schistosoma japonicum in the Philippines?
items.why: Each Schistosoma species depends on a specific snail genus. **In the Philippines, S. japonicum develops in the amphibious snail Oncomelania hupensis quadrasi**, and cercariae released into fresh water penetrate the skin of people who wade or work in it.

whyNot.0: Biomphalaria snails are intermediate hosts of Schistosoma mansoni, found in Africa, the Middle East, and South America.
whyNot.1: Bulinus snails are intermediate hosts of Schistosoma haematobium, the urinary schistosome.
whyNot.3: Lymnaeid snails are intermediate hosts of Fasciola species, not schistosomes.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Schistosoma japonicum chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Schistosomiasis

items.stem: A farmer from a paragonimiasis-endemic province has a chronic cough with rusty-brown, blood-streaked sputum and two negative AFB smears. A sputum wet mount shows yellow-brown operculated eggs about 90 × 55 µm with a flattened operculum set into a shell rim and a thickened end opposite the operculum. How was this infection most likely acquired?
options: Eating raw or undercooked freshwater crabs
Wading in fresh water where cercariae penetrated the skin
Eating raw aquatic plants such as watercress
items.why: The eggs are those of Paragonimus westermani, the lung fluke that can mimic pulmonary tuberculosis. **Humans are infected by eating raw or undercooked freshwater crabs containing metacercariae.** Eggs may appear in sputum or, if swallowed, in stool.

whyNot.1: Skin penetration by cercariae is the route for schistosomes, whose eggs have no operculum.
whyNot.2: Raw freshwater fish transmit Clonorchis, Opisthorchis, and Capillaria philippinensis, not Paragonimus.
whyNot.3: Aquatic plants carry metacercariae of Fasciola and Fasciolopsis, whose eggs are much larger and are found in stool.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Paragonimus chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Paragonimiasis

items.stem: Taenia eggs are found in a stool concentrate. Which procedure allows identification to the species level?
options: Measuring the diameter of the eggs
Counting the hooklets of the oncosphere
Counting the main lateral uterine branches of a gravid proglottid
Looking for polar filaments between the oncosphere and the shell
items.why: Eggs of T. solium and T. saginata look the same, so species identification relies on proglottids, the scolex, or molecular methods. **T. solium gravid proglottids have about 7–13 main lateral uterine branches per side, while T. saginata typically has more (about 12–30).** Because T. solium eggs can cause cysticercosis in humans, Taenia eggs should always be handled as infectious.

whyNot.0: Eggs of both species measure about 30–35 µm and have the same thick, radially striated shell, so size cannot separate them.
whyNot.1: All Taenia oncospheres carry six hooklets (three pairs), so counting them does not help.
whyNot.3: Polar filaments are a feature of Hymenolepis nana eggs; Taenia eggs do not have them.

items.ref: CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Taeniasis; Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Taenia chapter

items.stem: A trichrome-stained stool smear shows amoebae with a small central karyosome and fine, evenly spread peripheral chromatin. Which additional finding allows the laboratory to favor Entamoeba histolytica rather than reporting "E. histolytica/E. dispar"?
options: Trophozoites that contain ingested red blood cells
Chromatoid bodies with smooth, rounded ends
items.why: E. histolytica (pathogenic) and E. dispar (nonpathogenic) look the same by light microscopy, so the usual report is "E. histolytica/E. dispar". **Trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells are presumptive evidence of E. histolytica**; confirmation uses an E. histolytica-specific antigen test or PCR.

whyNot.0: Both species form mature cysts with four nuclei.
whyNot.2: Chromatoid bodies with smooth, rounded ends are seen in cysts of both E. histolytica and E. dispar.
whyNot.3: The trophozoite sizes of the two species overlap widely, so size cannot separate them.

items.ref: CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Amebiasis; Garcia, Diagnostic Medical Parasitology, 6th ed., intestinal amebae chapter

items.stem: A thin blood smear shows red cells of normal size, many carrying two or more small, delicate rings, some rings pressed against the cell edge, and crescent-shaped gametocytes. No mature schizonts are seen. Which species is most likely?
items.why: In P. falciparum infection, usually only rings and gametocytes circulate, because the later stages sequester in deep capillaries. **Crescent-shaped (banana-shaped) gametocytes are diagnostic of P. falciparum**, and multiple rings per cell and appliqué forms in normal-sized red cells support it.

whyNot.1: P. vivax enlarges the infected red cell, shows Schüffner's dots, and has all stages, including schizonts, in peripheral blood; its gametocytes are round.
whyNot.2: P. malariae has compact band-form trophozoites in normal or small red cells and rosette schizonts; its gametocytes are round.
whyNot.3: P. ovale enlarges the red cell, often making it oval with fringed edges and Schüffner's dots, and its gametocytes are round.

items.ref: CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Malaria; Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Plasmodium chapter

items.stem: A Kato-Katz thick smear is prepared during a soil-transmitted helminth survey. To avoid underestimating hookworm infection, when should the slide be examined?
options: After 24 hours, once the glycerol has fully cleared the fecal debris
Only after Lugol's iodine has been added to stain the eggs
At any time within a week, because helminth eggs do not change in glycerol
items.why: In the Kato-Katz method, a glycerol-soaked cellophane strip (with malachite green or methylene blue) clears the stool so eggs can be counted. **Thin-shelled hookworm eggs over-clear and become invisible after about 30–60 minutes**, whereas Ascaris and Trichuris eggs remain visible much longer. With the standard 41.7-mg template, the egg count is multiplied by 24 to give eggs per gram.

whyNot.1: Waiting longer helps clear the background, but by 24 hours most hookworm eggs have disappeared.
whyNot.2: Kato-Katz does not use iodine; the cellophane is soaked in glycerol with malachite green or methylene blue.
whyNot.3: Ascaris and Trichuris eggs keep for a long time, but hookworm eggs are destroyed quickly by the clearing process.

items.ref: WHO, Bench Aids for the Diagnosis of Intestinal Parasites, 2nd ed. (2019), Kato-Katz technique; Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., diagnostic techniques chapter

items.stem: A child has perianal itching at night and Enterobius vermicularis is suspected. Which specimen is most appropriate?
options: A routine stool sample for ova and parasite examination
A perianal cellulose-tape preparation collected in the evening after the child's bath
A perianal cellulose-tape preparation collected on waking, before bathing or defecation
Stool preserved in PVA for a permanent trichrome stain
items.why: The female pinworm migrates out at night to lay eggs on the perianal skin, so eggs are rarely found in stool. **A cellulose-tape preparation taken first thing in the morning, before bathing or using the toilet, gives the best yield**, and several consecutive daily samples may be needed to rule out infection.

whyNot.0: Pinworm eggs are deposited on the perianal skin rather than released into the bowel, so routine stool examinations usually miss them.
whyNot.1: Bathing removes the eggs laid overnight, and in the evening egg-laying has not yet taken place.
whyNot.3: PVA-preserved stool with trichrome stain is used to identify intestinal protozoa, not pinworm eggs.

items.ref: CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Enterobiasis; Garcia, Diagnostic Medical Parasitology, 6th ed., specimen collection chapter

items.stem: Which practice is correct for the ocular micrometer used to measure parasites?
options: Use calibration factors from another microscope of the same model
Calibrate only the 10× objective and derive the other factors by proportion
Calibrate once at purchase, even if the optics are later replaced
Calibrate each objective separately, and again when optics change
items.why: Size is often the deciding feature in parasite identification, so the ocular micrometer must be calibrated against a stage micrometer. **Each objective on each microscope must be calibrated separately**, and calibration is repeated whenever an objective or eyepiece is replaced; the factors should be posted on the microscope.

whyNot.0: Actual magnification differs between instruments, even of the same model, so each microscope needs its own calibration.
whyNot.1: Nominal magnifications are not exact, so a factor derived by proportion can give wrong measurements; each objective is calibrated directly.
whyNot.2: Replacing an objective or eyepiece changes the magnification, so the old calibration no longer applies.

items.ref: Garcia, Diagnostic Medical Parasitology, 6th ed., quality control and ocular micrometer calibration; CLSI M28 (Procedures for the Recovery and Identification of Parasites from the Intestinal Tract)

items.stem: A Gram stain of an expectorated sputum sent for routine bacterial culture shows many squamous epithelial cells and very few neutrophils per low-power field. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reject it and request a new, properly collected specimen
Culture it and report every organism that grows
Culture it anaerobically to look for aspiration pathogens
Culture it but report only the organism that predominates
items.why: Squamous epithelial cells come from the mouth, so their abundance shows that the sample is mostly saliva, and the scarcity of neutrophils shows that the lower airway was not sampled. **Many squamous epithelial cells mark oropharyngeal contamination**, so a culture would mainly grow oral flora and could mislead treatment. The laboratory should reject the specimen and ask for a deep-cough sample.

whyNot.1: Reporting everything that grows would list oral flora as if they were pathogens; the Gram-stain screen exists to stop exactly this.
whyNot.2: Expectorated sputum is never acceptable for anaerobic culture because the mouth is full of anaerobes.
whyNot.3: In a saliva-contaminated sample the predominant organism is often oral flora, so choosing it does not fix the poor specimen.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., lower respiratory tract infections chapter (sputum screening); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., lower respiratory tract chapter

items.stem: Fluid thioglycollate broth supports the growth of anaerobes as well as aerobes. What is the main role of sodium thioglycollate in this medium?
options: It is the redox indicator that turns pink where oxygen is present
It inhibits gram-positive bacteria so gram-negative rods can be recovered
It supplies hemin and vitamin K needed by pigmented anaerobes
It acts as a reducing agent that lowers the oxidation-reduction potential
items.why: Sodium thioglycollate removes dissolved oxygen and keeps the medium reduced, so obligate anaerobes can grow in the lower part of the tube. **Thioglycollate is a reducing agent**, and the small amount of agar in the broth slows the movement of oxygen back into the medium.

whyNot.0: The pink color at the top of the tube comes from the redox indicator, usually resazurin, not from thioglycollate.
whyNot.1: Thioglycollate broth is an all-purpose enriched medium, not a selective one; it supports both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.
whyNot.2: Hemin and vitamin K are supplements added to make enriched thioglycollate; they are not the function of the thioglycollate salt.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., culture media chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., anaerobic bacteriology chapter

items.stem: On xylose-lysine-deoxycholate (XLD) agar, Salmonella usually forms red colonies with black centers even though it ferments xylose. Why are the colonies red rather than yellow?
options: After xylose runs out, lysine decarboxylation forms amines that raise the pH
Fermentation of lactose and sucrose turns the phenol red indicator red
Hydrogen sulfide production masks the acid formed around the colony
Deamination of peptones by Salmonella forms ammonia that neutralizes the acid
items.why: Salmonella ferments the small amount of xylose first, then decarboxylates lysine, and the resulting amines return the phenol red indicator to its alkaline red color. **The red color comes from lysine decarboxylation after xylose is used up**, while the black centers come from hydrogen sulfide reacting with ferric ammonium citrate.

whyNot.1: Salmonella does not ferment lactose or sucrose, and sugar fermentation produces acid, which turns phenol red yellow, not red.
whyNot.2: Hydrogen sulfide only produces the black centers; it does not change the pH reaction of the colony.
whyNot.3: Deamination of amino acids is typical of Proteus, Morganella, and Providencia, not Salmonella, and it is not why Salmonella colonies turn red on XLD.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Enterobacteriaceae chapter (selective and differential media); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: CSF from a 5-day-old infant grows small gray colonies with a narrow zone of beta hemolysis. The isolate is a catalase-negative, gram-positive coccus in chains that is CAMP test positive and hydrolyzes hippurate. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Group B streptococcus is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis acquired from the mother's genital tract. **A positive CAMP test and hippurate hydrolysis in a beta-hemolytic, catalase-negative coccus** identify Streptococcus agalactiae.

whyNot.0: Streptococcus pyogenes is CAMP negative and hippurate negative; it is recognized instead by PYR positivity and bacitracin susceptibility.
whyNot.2: Listeria is also CAMP positive and causes neonatal meningitis, but it is a catalase-positive gram-positive rod, not a coccus in chains.
whyNot.3: Enterococcus faecalis is usually nonhemolytic on sheep blood agar and is identified by bile esculin hydrolysis and growth in 6.5% NaCl.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Streptococcus and Enterococcus chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Streptococcus chapter

items.stem: A catalase-negative, gram-positive coccus from a urine culture is bile esculin positive. Which additional result best indicates Enterococcus rather than a non-enterococcal group D streptococcus such as Streptococcus gallolyticus?
options: Reaction with Lancefield group D antiserum
items.why: Both enterococci and the Streptococcus bovis/gallolyticus group hydrolyze esculin in the presence of bile, so a second test is needed. **Enterococci grow in 6.5% NaCl, whereas the non-enterococcal group D streptococci do not**; a positive PYR test also supports Enterococcus.

whyNot.0: Blackening of bile esculin agar is the positive result already described; both groups give it, so it cannot separate them.
whyNot.2: Both genera can carry the group D antigen, so a positive group D reaction does not separate them.
whyNot.3: Optochin susceptibility identifies Streptococcus pneumoniae and plays no part in separating enterococci from other group D organisms.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Streptococcus and Enterococcus chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Enterococcus chapter

items.stem: Blood culture from a febrile pregnant woman grows a small, catalase-positive, gram-positive bacillus that shows a narrow zone of beta hemolysis on sheep blood agar. In semisolid motility medium held at about 25 °C, it forms an umbrella-shaped band of growth just below the surface. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Listeria is motile at room temperature but much less so at 35–37 °C, and it grows best just below the surface of semisolid agar because it is microaerophilic. **Umbrella-shaped motility at 25 °C in a catalase-positive, beta-hemolytic gram-positive rod** points to Listeria monocytogenes, a cause of bacteremia in pregnancy and of neonatal infection.

whyNot.0: Erysipelothrix is catalase negative and nonmotile, and it produces H2S in TSI.
whyNot.1: Bacillus cereus forms large rods with spores and large colonies with wide beta hemolysis; it is not the classic cause of bacteremia in pregnancy.
whyNot.2: Diphtheroids are catalase positive but are nonmotile and usually nonhemolytic.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., aerobic gram-positive bacilli chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Listeria and Erysipelothrix chapter

items.stem: Urine from a sexually active 20-year-old woman with cystitis grows a catalase-positive, coagulase-negative, gram-positive coccus in clusters. It is resistant to a 5-µg novobiocin disk. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infection in young, sexually active women. **Novobiocin resistance separates S. saprophyticus from most other clinically important coagulase-negative staphylococci**, which are susceptible.

whyNot.0: Staphylococcus epidermidis is novobiocin susceptible and is mainly a contaminant or a cause of device-related infection.
whyNot.2: Staphylococcus lugdunensis is novobiocin susceptible and is recognized by PYR and ornithine decarboxylase positivity.
whyNot.3: Staphylococcus haemolyticus is novobiocin susceptible.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Staphylococcus chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Staphylococcus chapter

items.stem: Large, very mucoid, pink colonies grow on MacConkey agar from the sputum of a patient with alcohol use disorder and lobar pneumonia. The isolate is nonmotile and gives these IMViC results: indole −, methyl red −, Voges-Proskauer +, citrate +. Which organism is this?
items.why: The IMViC pattern − − + + with lactose fermentation fits the Klebsiella-Enterobacter group, and the thick capsule gives very mucoid colonies. **Lack of motility** separates Klebsiella pneumoniae from Enterobacter and Serratia, which are motile.

whyNot.0: Escherichia coli gives the opposite IMViC pattern (+ + − −) and is usually motile.
whyNot.1: Enterobacter cloacae has the same IMViC pattern but is motile.
whyNot.2: Serratia marcescens is motile, ferments lactose slowly or not at all, and is DNase positive.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Enterobacteriaceae chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: A urine isolate swarms over sheep blood agar. It does not ferment lactose and is urease positive, phenylalanine deaminase positive, and H2S positive. Which result supports Proteus mirabilis rather than Proteus vulgaris?
options: Indole positive and ornithine decarboxylase negative
Indole negative and ornithine decarboxylase positive
items.why: Both species swarm, produce urease and H2S, and deaminate phenylalanine. **Proteus mirabilis is indole negative and ornithine decarboxylase positive**, whereas Proteus vulgaris is indole positive, ornithine negative, and ferments maltose.

whyNot.0: This is the pattern of Proteus vulgaris.
whyNot.1: Phenylalanine deaminase is positive in both species (and in Morganella and Providencia), so it does not separate them.
whyNot.2: Maltose fermentation is a feature of Proteus vulgaris, not P. mirabilis.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Enterobacteriaceae chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: A rice farmer with diabetes in Southeast Asia develops pneumonia and sepsis during the rainy season. Blood cultures grow an oxidase-positive, gram-negative bacillus with bipolar ("safety-pin") staining that forms dry, wrinkled colonies with an earthy odor after 2–3 days. It is resistant to gentamicin and colistin. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Melioidosis is acquired from soil and surface water in Southeast Asia, and diabetes is the main risk factor. **Wrinkled colonies plus resistance to both aminoglycosides and colistin in an oxidase-positive gram-negative rod** strongly suggest Burkholderia pseudomallei. Because it is a laboratory-acquired infection risk, cultures should be handled in a biological safety cabinet and the reference laboratory notified.

whyNot.1: Pseudomonas aeruginosa usually has a grape-like odor and blue-green pigment and is generally colistin susceptible.
whyNot.2: Pseudomonas stutzeri also forms dry, wrinkled colonies, but it is usually susceptible to aminoglycosides and colistin.
whyNot.3: Acinetobacter baumannii is oxidase negative and appears as plump coccobacilli.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Burkholderia chapter

items.stem: A Staphylococcus aureus isolate tests erythromycin resistant and clindamycin susceptible by disk diffusion. With the two disks placed 15–26 mm apart, the clindamycin zone is flattened on the side facing the erythromycin disk. How should clindamycin be reported?
options: Susceptible, because the clindamycin zone is in the susceptible range
Susceptible, because the isolate has a macrolide-only efflux pump
Resistant, because the isolate must also be methicillin resistant
Resistant, because the isolate has inducible clindamycin resistance
items.why: Erythromycin induces erm-encoded ribosomal methylation, which also blocks clindamycin, so the zone is flattened into a "D" next to the erythromycin disk. **A positive D-test means inducible clindamycin resistance**, and clindamycin is reported as resistant because therapy may fail.

whyNot.0: The zone size alone misses inducible resistance; that is why the D-test is done on erythromycin-resistant, clindamycin-susceptible staphylococci.
whyNot.1: A macrolide efflux pump (msrA) gives a round clindamycin zone (negative D-test); a flattened zone shows erm-mediated resistance.
whyNot.2: Inducible clindamycin resistance is unrelated to mecA; MSSA and MRSA can both be D-test positive.

items.ref: CLSI M100 (Performance Standards for Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing), inducible clindamycin resistance test; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., antimicrobial susceptibility testing chapter

items.stem: A Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate has reduced zones around third-generation cephalosporins. In the CLSI phenotypic confirmatory test, ceftazidime and cefotaxime disks are tested alone and with clavulanate. Which result confirms an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)?
options: A zone decrease of ≥5 mm with clavulanate for either agent
Cefoxitin resistance with no zone change when clavulanate is added
A zone increase of ≥5 mm with clavulanate for either agent
A cloverleaf-shaped indentation in a modified Hodge test
items.why: ESBLs are inhibited by clavulanate, so adding it restores activity of the cephalosporin and enlarges the zone. **An increase of 5 mm or more for either agent tested with clavulanate** confirms ESBL production.

whyNot.0: Clavulanate inhibits ESBLs, so it enlarges zones; a smaller zone is not the expected ESBL result.
whyNot.1: Cefoxitin resistance that clavulanate does not reverse suggests an AmpC β-lactamase, which is not inhibited by clavulanate.
whyNot.3: The modified Hodge test was a phenotypic screen for carbapenemases, not ESBLs.

items.ref: CLSI M100, ESBL phenotypic confirmatory test; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., antimicrobial susceptibility testing chapter

items.stem: Which disk does CLSI recommend as a surrogate in disk diffusion for detecting mecA-mediated oxacillin (methicillin) resistance in Staphylococcus aureus?
items.why: Cefoxitin strongly induces the mecA gene and gives clearer results than oxacillin for staphylococci by disk diffusion. **The cefoxitin disk is the surrogate disk test for methicillin resistance in S. aureus**; resistant isolates are reported as resistant to the penicillinase-stable β-lactams.

whyNot.0: The oxacillin 1-µg disk is the screen for penicillin resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae; for staphylococci it is less reliable than cefoxitin by disk diffusion.
whyNot.2: Penicillin resistance in staphylococci is mainly due to penicillinase and does not show whether mecA is present.
whyNot.3: Vancomycin disk diffusion is not reliable for staphylococci, and vancomycin is unrelated to mecA.

items.ref: CLSI M100, Staphylococcus spp. (cefoxitin surrogate for oxacillin); Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., antimicrobial susceptibility testing chapter

items.stem: An anaerobic gram-negative bacillus from an intra-abdominal abscess grows well on Bacteroides bile esculin (BBE) agar, forming gray colonies surrounded by a dark brown-black zone. What does this result show?
options: Black pigment formed from hemin, typical of Porphyromonas species
Lipase activity on the medium, typical of Fusobacterium necrophorum
Tolerance of bile, typical of the pigmented Prevotella species
Bile tolerance and esculin hydrolysis, typical of the B. fragilis group
items.why: BBE agar contains 20% bile, esculin, ferric ammonium citrate, and gentamicin. **Organisms of the Bacteroides fragilis group tolerate bile and hydrolyze esculin**, and the esculetin formed reacts with iron to give the brown-black zone.

whyNot.0: Porphyromonas makes its pigment slowly on blood-containing media, and it is inhibited by bile so it does not grow on BBE.
whyNot.1: Lipase is detected as an iridescent sheen on egg yolk agar, not as blackening on BBE.
whyNot.2: Prevotella species are inhibited by bile, which is one way they are separated from the B. fragilis group.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., anaerobes chapter (selective media); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., anaerobic bacteriology chapter

items.stem: In the N-acetyl-L-cysteine–sodium hydroxide (NALC-NaOH) method for processing sputum for mycobacterial culture, what is the function of NALC?
options: It liquefies mucus so the specimen can be decontaminated and concentrated
It kills the contaminating normal flora that would overgrow the culture
It neutralizes the sodium hydroxide before the specimen is centrifuged
It inactivates mycobacteria so the specimen can be handled on an open bench
items.why: Thick sputum traps mycobacteria and shields contaminants from the decontaminating agent. **NALC is a mucolytic agent**, while NaOH is the decontaminant; phosphate buffer then dilutes and neutralizes the NaOH before centrifugation.

whyNot.1: Killing the contaminating flora is the job of NaOH, not NALC.
whyNot.2: Dilution and neutralization are done with phosphate buffer (and pH adjustment), not with NALC.
whyNot.3: NALC-NaOH processing does not reliably kill mycobacteria; specimens must still be handled in a biological safety cabinet.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Mycobacterium chapter (specimen processing); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Mycobacteria chapter

items.stem: A resident of a flood-prone barangay develops fever, severe calf pain, and conjunctival suffusion 10 days after wading through floodwater. He is seen on the third day of illness. Which specimen is most likely to yield Leptospira by culture at this stage?
items.why: During the first week of illness leptospires circulate in the blood, and they are cultured in special media such as EMJH or Fletcher's semisolid medium. **Blood is the specimen of choice during the first (leptospiremic) week**, and blood should be collected before antibiotics are given.

whyNot.0: Leptospires usually appear in urine from the second week on, so urine is better later in the illness.
whyNot.1: Leptospirosis is not an intestinal infection, and stool is not used to recover the organism.
whyNot.3: Even in pulmonary hemorrhage, sputum is not used for Leptospira culture; it is contaminated with oral flora.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., spirochetes chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Leptospira chapter

items.stem: Why are infections caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae not treated with penicillins or cephalosporins?
options: The organism is an obligate intracellular parasite
The organism has no cell wall
The organism has an outer membrane that excludes these drugs
items.why: β-lactam drugs act by blocking peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis. **Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall**, so these drugs have no target; macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones are used instead. The lack of a wall also explains why the organism does not stain with the Gram stain.

whyNot.0: Resistance is not due to a β-lactamase; there is simply no peptidoglycan for the drug to act on.
whyNot.1: Mycoplasma can grow on cell-free media; obligate intracellular growth describes Chlamydia and Rickettsia.
whyNot.3: An outer membrane is a feature of gram-negative bacteria; Mycoplasma has only a sterol-containing cell membrane.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Chlamydia, Rickettsia, and Mycoplasma chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma chapter

items.stem: Skin scrapings from the active border of a ringworm lesion are collected for fungal culture. How should they be sent to the laboratory?
options: In a sealed tube of sterile saline
On a swab in Amies bacterial transport medium
In a clean, dry paper envelope or folded paper
In a closed plastic bag kept in the refrigerator
items.why: Dermatophytes survive well in dry keratin, while moisture lets contaminating bacteria and fast-growing molds multiply. **Skin, hair, and nail specimens are sent dry in a clean paper envelope or folded paper**, after the site has been wiped with 70% alcohol.

whyNot.0: Saline keeps the specimen moist and encourages overgrowth of contaminants.
whyNot.1: Bacterial transport swabs pick up little keratin and keep the material moist; scrapings are preferred.
whyNot.3: Closed plastic containers trap moisture, and dermatophyte specimens do not need refrigeration.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., mycology chapter (specimen collection); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., laboratory methods in basic mycology chapter

items.stem: A dermatophyte from a toenail forms a khaki-yellow, velvety colony. Microscopy shows smooth, thin-walled, club-shaped macroconidia in clusters of two or three, and no microconidia. Which organism is it?
items.why: Epidermophyton floccosum infects skin and nails but not hair. **Clusters of smooth, club-shaped macroconidia with no microconidia** identify this genus.

whyNot.0: Microsporum canis has thick-walled, rough, spindle-shaped macroconidia with many cells.
whyNot.1: Trichophyton rubrum produces many teardrop-shaped microconidia along the hyphae, and its colonies usually have a red reverse.
whyNot.3: Trichophyton tonsurans produces many microconidia of varying shapes, including enlarged balloon forms.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., mycology chapter (dermatophytes); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., dermatophytes chapter

items.stem: Which hepatitis virus is defective and can form infectious particles only in a person who is also infected with hepatitis B virus?
items.why: Hepatitis D virus has a small circular RNA genome but no envelope protein of its own. **HDV uses HBsAg as its envelope**, so it can only spread as a coinfection with HBV or as a superinfection of an HBV carrier.

whyNot.0: Hepatitis A virus is a complete enteric RNA virus spread by the fecal-oral route.
whyNot.2: Hepatitis C virus is a complete enveloped RNA virus that replicates on its own.
whyNot.3: Hepatitis E virus is a complete enteric virus; it is known for severe disease in pregnant women, not for depending on HBV.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., viruses chapter (hepatitis viruses); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., hepatitis viruses chapter

items.stem: A swab is chosen to collect a nasopharyngeal specimen for respiratory virus culture or PCR. Which swab is preferred?
options: A flocked synthetic swab on a plastic shaft
A cotton-tipped swab on a wooden shaft
A calcium alginate swab on an aluminum shaft
A charcoal-impregnated swab in Amies medium
items.why: Some swab materials are toxic to viruses or inhibit nucleic acid amplification. **Synthetic tips (such as flocked nylon, Dacron, or rayon) on thin plastic or wire shafts** are recommended, placed in viral transport medium.

whyNot.1: Wooden shafts and cotton tips can contain substances that inactivate viruses and inhibit PCR.
whyNot.2: Calcium alginate is toxic to some viruses (such as herpes simplex) and inhibits PCR; the problem is the alginate tip, since thin wire shafts are acceptable.
whyNot.3: Charcoal swabs are designed to protect fastidious bacteria, and charcoal can interfere with viral testing.

items.ref: CDC, Interim Guidelines for Collecting and Handling Clinical Specimens for COVID-19 Testing (swab types); Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., viruses chapter (specimen collection)

items.stem: Primary rhesus monkey kidney cells inoculated with a nasopharyngeal specimen show no cytopathic effect after 5 days. When guinea pig red blood cells are added, they stick to the cell monolayer. Which virus is most likely present?
items.why: Infected cells express viral hemagglutinin on their surface, so red cells attach even before any cytopathic effect is visible. **Hemadsorption in monkey kidney cells detects viruses with a surface hemagglutinin**, such as parainfluenza virus and influenza virus.

whyNot.1: RSV does not have a hemagglutinin and is recognized by syncytia in HEp-2 cells.
whyNot.2: Adenovirus produces grapelike clusters of swollen, rounded cells in HEp-2 or A549 cells and does not hemadsorb in this test.
whyNot.3: Rhinovirus causes cytopathic effect in human fibroblast cells and does not hemadsorb.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., viruses chapter (cell culture and hemadsorption); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., laboratory methods in virology chapter

items.stem: The cartridge-based real-time PCR assay Xpert MTB/RIF, used by many national TB programs including the Philippines', detects M. tuberculosis complex and predicts rifampicin resistance. Mutations in which gene does it detect?
items.why: Rifampicin binds the β subunit of RNA polymerase, and most resistant strains have mutations in a short region of its gene. **Xpert MTB/RIF detects mutations in the 81-bp rifampicin resistance–determining region of rpoB** using molecular beacon probes.

whyNot.0: katG mutations cause high-level isoniazid resistance and are not targeted by Xpert MTB/RIF.
whyNot.1: inhA mutations cause low-level isoniazid and ethionamide resistance; line probe assays detect them, not Xpert MTB/RIF.
whyNot.2: embB mutations are linked to ethambutol resistance.

items.ref: WHO, Xpert MTB/RIF implementation manual; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Mycobacterium chapter (molecular methods)

items.stem: A hospital laboratory prepares its annual cumulative antibiogram to guide empiric therapy and support resistance surveillance. Following CLSI M39 guidance, which isolates should be included?
options: Every isolate tested, including repeat isolates from the same patient
Only isolates that were resistant to at least one antimicrobial
Only isolates recovered from blood cultures
Only the first isolate of each species per patient in the period
items.why: Repeat cultures from patients with long, complicated infections tend to be resistant and would skew the data. **CLSI M39 includes only the first diagnostic isolate of a species per patient per analysis period**, regardless of specimen source, and recommends at least 30 isolates per species.

whyNot.0: Including repeat isolates over-represents chronically infected patients and makes resistance look higher.
whyNot.1: Leaving out susceptible isolates would make every percentage meaningless.
whyNot.2: M39 counts isolates from all clinical specimen types; blood-only tables can be made as a supplement.

items.ref: CLSI M39 (Analysis and Presentation of Cumulative Antimicrobial Susceptibility Test Data); Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., antimicrobial susceptibility testing chapter

items.stem: Which activity in a microbiology laboratory is a quality assurance indicator rather than a quality control procedure?
options: Testing a new lot of MacConkey agar with known control strains
Checking the Gram stain reagents daily with known gram-positive and gram-negative organisms
Tracking the monthly blood culture contamination rate
Testing a new lot of antimicrobial disks with an ATCC reference strain
items.why: Quality control checks whether a specific test, reagent, or medium performs correctly, while quality assurance monitors the whole testing process, including pre- and post-analytic steps. **The blood culture contamination rate reflects collection practice and patient outcomes**, so it is a QA indicator.

whyNot.0: Checking a new media lot with control strains is a quality control procedure for that reagent.
whyNot.1: Daily Gram stain control slides are quality control of the stain reagents.
whyNot.3: Testing antimicrobial disks with reference strains is quality control of the susceptibility test.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., quality in the clinical microbiology laboratory chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., quality in the clinical microbiology laboratory chapter

items.stem: A child from a rural barangay with chronic bloody diarrhea and rectal prolapse passes stool containing barrel-shaped, yellow-brown eggs about 50 × 22 µm with a clear plug at each end. Which parasite is most likely?
items.why: Whipworm eggs are barrel or lemon shaped, bile stained, and have prominent bipolar plugs. **Heavy Trichuris infection in children can cause dysentery and rectal prolapse**.

whyNot.0: Enterobius eggs are colorless, flattened on one side, and have no polar plugs; they are found with the tape test.
whyNot.1: Capillaria philippinensis eggs are peanut-shaped with a striated shell and flattened, inconspicuous plugs, and the disease causes watery diarrhea.
whyNot.3: Ascaris eggs are round to oval with a thick, bumpy (mammillated) outer coat and no plugs.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Trichuris trichiura chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Trichuriasis

items.stem: Adult hookworms passed after treatment are examined. The buccal capsule has a pair of cutting plates instead of teeth. Which species is it?
items.why: Hookworm eggs cannot be told apart, but adult worms can be identified by their mouthparts. **Necator americanus has cutting plates, whereas Ancylostoma species have teeth.**

whyNot.0: Ancylostoma duodenale has two pairs of ventral teeth.
whyNot.2: Ancylostoma braziliense, a cause of cutaneous larva migrans, has teeth (one large and one small pair).
whyNot.3: Ancylostoma caninum, the dog hookworm, has three pairs of teeth.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., hookworm chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Hookworm (intestinal)

items.stem: A Giemsa-stained thick blood film collected near midnight shows a sheathed microfilaria. The sheath stains pink, and the tail has two distinct terminal nuclei separated by a gap. Which species is it?
items.why: Blood for lymphatic filariae with nocturnal periodicity is drawn at night, when microfilariae are most numerous. **Two separate terminal nuclei in the tail and a sheath that stains pink with Giemsa** identify Brugia malayi.

whyNot.0: Wuchereria bancrofti has no nuclei in the tip of the tail, and its sheath stains poorly with Giemsa.
whyNot.1: Loa loa is sheathed but has nuclei running continuously to the tail tip, and it shows daytime periodicity.
whyNot.3: Mansonella perstans is unsheathed, with nuclei extending to a blunt tail tip.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., filarial worms chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Lymphatic Filariasis

items.stem: Several adults in a rural town develop severe headache and neck stiffness about 2 weeks after eating raw freshwater snails (kuhol). Their CSF shows marked eosinophilia. Which parasite is most likely responsible?
items.why: Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the rat lungworm, develops in snails and slugs as intermediate hosts. **Eating raw snails followed by eosinophilic meningitis** is its classic presentation, as the larvae migrate to the brain.

whyNot.0: Gnathostoma also causes eosinophilic meningitis, but it is acquired from undercooked fish, frogs, or poultry, not snails.
whyNot.1: Echinostoma ilocanum is acquired from snails but is an intestinal fluke and does not cause meningitis.
whyNot.2: Toxocara canis is acquired by swallowing eggs from soil contaminated by dog feces and causes visceral or ocular larva migrans.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Angiostrongylus cantonensis chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Angiostrongyliasis

items.stem: Stool from a farmer living in a schistosomiasis-endemic area of the Philippines contains nonoperculated oval eggs about 70–100 × 55–65 µm with a small, inconspicuous lateral knob. Which species is most likely?
items.why: Schistosoma japonicum is the only schistosome endemic in the Philippines. **Its eggs are rounder than other schistosome eggs and have only a tiny lateral knob**, which is often hard to see.

whyNot.1: Schistosoma mansoni eggs are elongated with a large, prominent lateral spine, and the species is not endemic in the Philippines.
whyNot.2: Schistosoma haematobium eggs have a terminal spine and are usually found in urine.
whyNot.3: Fasciola hepatica eggs are larger (about 130–150 µm) and have an operculum.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Schistosoma japonicum chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Schistosomiasis

items.stem: Neurocysticercosis is diagnosed in a woman who has never eaten pork. How was she most likely infected?
options: By eating undercooked beef containing Taenia cysticerci
By swallowing Taenia solium eggs shed by a human tapeworm carrier
By eating raw freshwater fish containing plerocercoid larvae
By drinking water containing infected copepods
items.why: Humans develop cysticercosis when they swallow Taenia solium eggs, which hatch and send larvae to tissues such as the brain. **Eating pork with cysticerci causes the intestinal tapeworm, but cysticercosis comes from swallowing eggs**, often from food handled by a carrier.

whyNot.0: Beef cysticerci belong to Taenia saginata, which causes only intestinal taeniasis and not human cysticercosis.
whyNot.2: Plerocercoids in fish transmit Diphyllobothrium (Dibothriocephalus) tapeworms, not cysticercosis.
whyNot.3: Infected copepods transmit Dracunculus or Spirometra (sparganosis), not cysticercosis.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Taenia solium chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Cysticercosis

items.stem: A stool wet mount shows pear-shaped flagellate trophozoites with two nuclei, a ventral sucking disk, and "falling leaf" motility. Which parasite is it?
items.why: Giardia duodenalis (G. lamblia) attaches to the duodenal lining with its ventral disk and causes fatty diarrhea and malabsorption. **Two nuclei giving a "face-like" look, a sucking disk, and falling-leaf motility** are its distinctive features.

whyNot.1: Chilomastix has a single nucleus, a prominent cytostome, and a spiral groove, and it moves with a rotary motion.
whyNot.2: Trichomonas hominis has one nucleus and an undulating membrane running the length of the body, and it moves jerkily.
whyNot.3: Dientamoeba is often binucleate but moves like an amoeba and has no visible flagella or sucking disk.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., intestinal flagellates chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Giardiasis

items.stem: A patient treated for Plasmodium vivax malaria with a blood-stage drug alone has another attack several months later without being re-exposed to mosquitoes. Which stage is responsible?
items.why: Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale can leave dormant liver stages that reactivate weeks to months later. **Relapse comes from hypnozoites**, so radical cure needs a drug active against liver stages, such as primaquine, in addition to blood schizonticides.

whyNot.1: Gametocytes infect mosquitoes; they do not multiply in the human host and cannot cause a new attack.
whyNot.2: Sequestration of mature stages in deep capillaries is a feature of P. falciparum and does not explain a later relapse.
whyNot.3: Survival of blood-stage parasites causes recrudescence, not relapse; vivax relapse arises from the liver.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Plasmodium chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Malaria

items.stem: Stool from an HIV patient with profuse watery diarrhea is stained with a modified acid-fast (Kinyoun) stain. It shows round, pink-red oocysts about 4–6 µm across, some with a few dark granules, on a blue background. Which organism is most likely?
items.why: Cryptosporidium is an important cause of chronic watery diarrhea in people with AIDS. **Small, round, acid-fast oocysts of about 4–6 µm** are typical of Cryptosporidium.

whyNot.0: Cyclospora oocysts are larger (about 8–10 µm), stain variably with acid-fast stains, and fluoresce under UV light.
whyNot.2: Cystoisospora belli oocysts are much larger (about 20–33 µm) and elongated or ellipsoidal.
whyNot.3: Microsporidial spores are only about 1–2 µm and are best seen with a modified trichrome stain.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., coccidia chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Cryptosporidiosis

items.stem: Why is formalin-ethyl acetate sedimentation often preferred over zinc sulfate flotation when a laboratory uses only one concentration method for ova and parasite examination?
options: It gives a cleaner preparation with less fecal debris
It recovers operculated and infertile eggs that may not float
It keeps protozoan trophozoites alive and motile
It recovers eggs from the surface film without centrifugation
items.why: Heavy eggs, such as operculated trematode and cestode eggs and infertile Ascaris eggs, may sink or collapse in flotation solutions. **Sedimentation recovers all groups of parasites**, making it the more reliable single routine method.

whyNot.0: Flotation actually gives the cleaner preparation; sedimentation leaves more debris.
whyNot.2: Formalin kills and fixes parasites, so trophozoites are not motile in either concentrate.
whyNot.3: Collecting the surface film describes flotation, and formalin-ethyl acetate sedimentation uses centrifugation.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., laboratory diagnosis chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Diagnostic Procedures — Stool Specimens (concentration)

items.stem: The laboratory receives external proficiency-testing samples for ova and parasite examination. How should they be handled?
options: Examined only by the most experienced parasitologist to ensure a passing score
Sent to a reference laboratory for confirmation before results are submitted
Examined by staff who routinely do O&P tests, in the same way as patient samples
Examined repeatedly by several staff until all agree before submitting
items.why: Proficiency testing is meant to show how the laboratory performs on everyday specimens. **PT samples must be tested by the usual personnel using the routine methods**, without extra checks; sending them to another laboratory is prohibited.

whyNot.0: Assigning only the best analyst gives a falsely good picture of routine performance.
whyNot.1: Referring PT samples to another laboratory is prohibited and defeats the purpose of external assessment.
whyNot.3: Repeated testing by several people is not how patient samples are handled, so the results would not reflect real performance.

items.ref: Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., quality in the clinical microbiology laboratory chapter; Garcia, Diagnostic Medical Parasitology, 6th ed., quality systems chapter

items.stem: A clean-catch midstream urine for bacterial culture is collected at an outpatient clinic, but it cannot be plated for several hours. How should it be held until plating?
options: Kept at room temperature on the bench until it can be plated
Incubated at 35 °C so that low numbers of bacteria become detectable
Refrigerated at 2–8 °C and plated within 24 hours
Frozen at −20 °C and thawed just before it is plated
items.why: Because urine supports bacterial growth, unpreserved urine should be plated within about 2 hours of collection. If that is not possible, **refrigeration at 2–8 °C keeps the colony count stable for up to 24 hours**; a boric acid preservative tube is an alternative.

whyNot.0: Urine is a good growth medium; at room temperature bacteria multiply and falsely raise the colony count.
whyNot.1: Incubation lets organisms multiply, so the count no longer reflects the number in the bladder and may be misread as significant bacteriuria.
whyNot.3: Freezing and thawing can kill bacteria and is not used for routine urine culture specimens.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., urinary tract infections chapter (specimen transport); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., specimen management chapter

items.stem: When blood cultures are collected from an adult with suspected bacteremia, which factor most strongly affects the chance of recovering the organism?
options: Timing the draw to match the peak of a fever spike
Volume of blood added to the culture bottles
Drawing the sample through an existing intravenous catheter
Refrigerating the bottles until they are loaded into the instrument
items.why: Adults with bacteremia often have fewer than 1 organism per mL of blood, so the amount sampled determines whether an organism is caught. **The volume of blood cultured is the single most important factor in blood culture yield**, which is why adequately filled bottles and two or more sets are recommended.

whyNot.0: Organisms usually enter the blood before the fever rises and may be cleared by its peak; guidelines stress volume and number of sets, collected before antibiotics, rather than fever timing.
whyNot.2: Catheter draws have higher contamination rates; venipuncture is preferred unless catheter infection is being evaluated.
whyNot.3: Inoculated bottles should be kept at room temperature or loaded promptly; refrigeration can harm fastidious organisms and delays detection.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., bloodstream infections chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., bloodstream infections chapter

items.stem: Mannitol salt agar is used to screen specimens for Staphylococcus aureus. Which component makes the medium selective?
items.why: **The high salt concentration (7.5% NaCl) inhibits most bacteria except staphylococci**. Mannitol and phenol red make the medium differential: S. aureus ferments mannitol and its colonies are surrounded by a yellow zone.

whyNot.1: Mannitol is the differential ingredient; fermentation of it separates S. aureus from most coagulase-negative staphylococci but does not inhibit other bacteria.
whyNot.2: Phenol red is the pH indicator that turns yellow when mannitol is fermented; it has no selective action.
whyNot.3: Crystal violet is a selective agent in MacConkey agar, where it inhibits gram-positive organisms; it is not in mannitol salt agar.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., culture media chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., culture media chapter

items.stem: A throat swab from a child with pharyngitis grows beta-hemolytic, catalase-negative, gram-positive cocci in chains. Which pair of results supports Streptococcus pyogenes?
options: CAMP test positive and hippurate hydrolysis positive
Bile esculin positive and growth in 6.5% NaCl
items.why: Group A streptococci are susceptible to a 0.04-U bacitracin disk and hydrolyze L-pyrrolidonyl-β-naphthylamide. **S. pyogenes is the only common beta-hemolytic streptococcus that is PYR positive**, which helps because some group C and G strains are also bacitracin susceptible.

whyNot.0: These results identify Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), not group A.
whyNot.1: These results identify Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is alpha-hemolytic.
whyNot.2: These results identify Enterococcus, which is usually not beta-hemolytic.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Streptococcus and Enterococcus chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Streptococcus chapter

items.stem: A child with bloody diarrhea develops hemolytic uremic syndrome a few days later. The stool is plated on sorbitol-MacConkey (SMAC) agar. Which colonies should be picked for Escherichia coli O157:H7 testing?
options: Colorless colonies, because O157:H7 usually does not ferment sorbitol
Pink colonies, because O157:H7 ferments sorbitol rapidly
Colonies with black centers, because O157:H7 produces H2S
Colonies with a green sheen, because O157:H7 ferments lactose strongly
items.why: Most E. coli ferment sorbitol within 24 hours, but **E. coli O157:H7 typically does not ferment sorbitol and forms colorless colonies on SMAC**. These colonies are then tested with O157 antiserum. Shiga toxin testing is also advised because non-O157 Shiga toxin-producing strains ferment sorbitol.
