whyNot.1: Pink colonies are the usual sorbitol-fermenting E. coli of normal flora; picking them would miss O157:H7.
whyNot.2: SMAC has no H2S indicator, and E. coli is H2S negative; black centers are a Salmonella feature on media such as XLD or HE.
whyNot.3: The green metallic sheen appears on EMB agar with strong lactose fermenters; O157:H7 ferments lactose like other E. coli, so lactose does not separate it.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Enterobacterales chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: Stool from a patient with diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken is plated on a selective Campylobacter medium. Which incubation conditions are best for recovering Campylobacter jejuni?
options: 25 °C in ambient air with added CO2
items.why: C. jejuni is both microaerophilic and thermotolerant. **Incubation at 42 °C in about 5% O2, 10% CO2, and 85% N2** favors it while suppressing much of the fecal flora. Gram stain shows curved "gull-wing" rods, and C. jejuni is hippurate positive.

whyNot.0: C. jejuni is microaerophilic and does not grow in the 21% oxygen of room air.
whyNot.1: C. jejuni needs some oxygen and grows poorly or not at all under strict anaerobic conditions.
whyNot.3: C. jejuni does not grow at 25 °C; low-temperature incubation is used for Yersinia enterocolitica.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Campylobacter chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Campylobacter chapter

items.stem: A cattle farmer has a painless skin ulcer with a black eschar. Culture grows a large gram-positive bacillus with square ends in long chains. Which features support Bacillus anthracis rather than Bacillus cereus?
options: Motile, and beta-hemolytic on sheep blood agar
Catalase negative, and grows only under anaerobic conditions
Nonmotile, and nonhemolytic on sheep blood agar
Penicillin resistant, and forms a double zone of hemolysis
items.why: **B. anthracis is nonmotile and nonhemolytic**, forming gray, flat "Medusa head" colonies that stand up like beaten egg white when lifted with a loop. B. cereus is motile and beta-hemolytic. A suspected B. anthracis isolate is handled in a biological safety cabinet and referred to a reference laboratory.

whyNot.0: These are features of B. cereus and most other Bacillus species.
whyNot.1: Bacillus species are catalase positive and aerobic or facultative; strict anaerobic growth suggests Clostridium.
whyNot.3: B. cereus, not B. anthracis, is typically penicillin resistant, and the double zone of hemolysis is a Clostridium perfringens feature.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Bacillus chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Bacillus chapter

items.stem: A tracheal aspirate from a ventilated ICU patient grows a plump gram-negative coccobacillus that forms non-lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar. It is oxidase negative and nonmotile, and it gives an alkaline/alkaline (K/K) reaction on TSI. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: A K/K TSI reaction shows a nonfermenter. Among nonfermenters, **the combination of oxidase negative and nonmotile** points to Acinetobacter, a common cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia that is often multidrug resistant. Its coccobacilli may resist decolorization and look gram-variable.

whyNot.0: S. maltophilia is also an oxidase-negative nonfermenter, but it is motile and is DNase positive.
whyNot.2: P. aeruginosa is a nonfermenter but is oxidase positive and motile.
whyNot.3: Moraxella species are nonmotile coccobacilli but are oxidase positive and usually grow poorly or not at all on MacConkey agar.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Acinetobacter chapter

items.stem: Sputum from an older smoker with a COPD flare grows gray-white colonies that slide intact across the agar when pushed with a loop. Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci, and the isolate is oxidase positive. Which result best confirms Moraxella catarrhalis rather than a Neisseria species?
options: Acid production from both glucose and maltose
Acid production from glucose but not maltose
items.why: M. catarrhalis forms "hockey puck" colonies, produces no acid from carbohydrates, and is DNase and nitrate positive. **A positive butyrate esterase (tributyrin) test** is a rapid way to separate it from Neisseria species, which are negative.

whyNot.0: This pattern fits Neisseria meningitidis; M. catarrhalis produces no acid from carbohydrates.
whyNot.1: This pattern fits Neisseria gonorrhoeae; M. catarrhalis is asaccharolytic.
whyNot.3: Pathogenic Neisseria grow on this medium and some M. catarrhalis strains do too, so growth does not separate them.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Neisseria and Moraxella chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Neisseria and Moraxella catarrhalis chapter

items.stem: A Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate is resistant to meropenem. In the modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM), a meropenem disk is incubated in a broth suspension of the isolate and then placed on Mueller-Hinton agar seeded with a carbapenem-susceptible E. coli strain. Which result indicates carbapenemase production?
options: A wide zone, as large as that of an unexposed meropenem disk
A cloverleaf-shaped indentation of indicator growth toward a streak
An enlarged zone where a clavulanate disk is placed nearby
A small zone or no zone around the disk
items.why: If the isolate makes a carbapenemase, it hydrolyzes the meropenem in the disk during incubation, so the susceptible indicator E. coli grows close to the disk. **A zone of 6–15 mm (6 mm is the disk itself) is read as carbapenemase positive** under CLSI M100, while a zone of 19 mm or more is negative.

whyNot.0: An intact zone means the meropenem was not destroyed, so the result is negative; resistance may come from other mechanisms such as porin loss with AmpC or ESBL.
whyNot.1: This describes the modified Hodge test, an older and different method.
whyNot.2: Synergy with clavulanate is used to detect extended-spectrum β-lactamases, not carbapenemases.

items.ref: CLSI M100, Performance Standards for Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (current ed.), mCIM/eCIM section; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., antimicrobial susceptibility testing chapter

items.stem: A stool isolate from a child with dysentery is a non-lactose fermenter on MacConkey agar. TSI shows K/A with no gas and no H2S. The isolate is nonmotile, urease negative, and lysine decarboxylase negative. Which genus is most likely?
items.why: **A nonmotile, H2S-negative non-lactose fermenter that produces no gas** fits Shigella. The identification is confirmed biochemically and by serogrouping with Shigella antisera.

whyNot.1: Most Salmonella are motile, H2S positive, and lysine decarboxylase positive.
whyNot.2: Proteus is motile (often swarming), urease positive, and usually H2S positive.
whyNot.3: Yersinia enterocolitica is usually urease positive and is motile at 25 °C.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Enterobacterales chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: A hospitalized patient on antibiotics has three or more unformed stools a day. The laboratory uses a two-step algorithm for Clostridioides difficile. The glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) antigen screen is positive, but the toxin A/B immunoassay is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Report the patient as negative for C. difficile infection
Test the specimen with a nucleic acid amplification test for the toxin gene
Report C. difficile infection as confirmed by the positive GDH result
Repeat the GDH screen on a formed stool collected the next day
items.why: GDH is a sensitive screen but does not show toxin production, and toxin immunoassays are specific but insensitive. **Discordant GDH-positive, toxin-negative results are resolved by a NAAT for the toxin gene** (or by a cytotoxin or toxigenic culture method).

whyNot.0: Toxin immunoassays have limited sensitivity, so a negative toxin result alone cannot rule out infection when GDH is positive.
whyNot.2: GDH is made by both toxigenic and nontoxigenic strains, so it shows the organism is present but not that it makes toxin.
whyNot.3: Formed stools are not suitable for C. difficile testing, and repeating the screen does not resolve the discordance.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., anaerobes chapter (Clostridioides difficile); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Clostridium and Clostridioides chapter

items.stem: A slow-growing acid-fast bacillus from a patient with chronic lung disease forms buff colonies when grown in the dark. After the colonies are exposed to light and reincubated, they turn yellow. How is the organism classified, and which species fits?
items.why: In the Runyon scheme, **photochromogens make pigment only after exposure to light**. M. kansasii is the classic photochromogen; it causes a tuberculosis-like lung disease and typically shows long, banded rods on acid-fast stain.

whyNot.0: Scotochromogens are pigmented even when grown in the dark; M. gordonae is a common tap-water contaminant.
whyNot.1: Nonphotochromogens stay buff or only lightly pigmented whether or not they are exposed to light.
whyNot.2: Rapid growers form mature colonies within 7 days, and M. fortuitum is nonpigmented.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Mycobacterium chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Mycobacteria chapter

items.stem: A patient with severe pneumonia and low serum sodium had recently stayed in a hotel with a cooling tower. A faintly staining, thin gram-negative bacillus grows after 3 days on buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar. It does not grow on sheep blood agar or on BCYE lacking L-cysteine. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Legionella is acquired by inhaling aerosols from water systems. It grows slowly on BCYE, and its **requirement for L-cysteine** (with iron) is the basis for presumptively identifying a suspect isolate by its failure to grow without cysteine. Francisella tularensis is also cysteine dependent, so identification is confirmed by DFA, MALDI-TOF, or a reference laboratory.

whyNot.1: H. influenzae grows on chocolate agar within a day and needs X and V factors, not L-cysteine.
whyNot.2: B. pertussis is a tiny coccobacillus recovered on Regan-Lowe or Bordet-Gengou media from nasopharyngeal specimens, and it causes whooping cough rather than severe pneumonia linked to a water source.
whyNot.3: Mycoplasma has no cell wall, is not seen on Gram stain, and grows on special media such as SP4 as tiny fried-egg colonies.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Legionella chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., Legionella chapter

items.stem: A child has scaly patches of hair loss on the scalp, and tinea capitis is suspected. How should hair be collected for fungal culture?
options: Cut the affected hairs close to the scalp with sterile scissors
Pluck affected hairs with sterile forceps so the hair base is included
Collect loose hairs shed on the pillowcase overnight
Place the hairs in a sealed tube of sterile saline
items.why: Dermatophytes invade the hair shaft at and below the scalp surface. **Plucked hairs that include the base** (choosing hairs that fluoresce under a Wood's lamp when present) are sent dry in a paper envelope, together with scale from the lesion.

whyNot.0: Cut hairs leave behind the part of the shaft at and below the scalp, where the fungus is most concentrated.
whyNot.2: Shed hairs may come from uninvolved areas and are often contaminated, so they are unreliable.
whyNot.3: Moist transport encourages overgrowth of bacteria and contaminating molds; hair is sent dry.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., mycology chapter (specimen collection); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., laboratory methods in mycology chapter

items.stem: During a gastroenteritis outbreak on a hospital ward, infection control finds that alcohol-based hand rubs are not reliable against the agent, norovirus, and recommends soap-and-water handwashing and chlorine-based cleaning. Which property of norovirus explains this?
options: It has a double-stranded DNA genome
It forms spores that survive in the environment
It carries its own reverse transcriptase
items.why: Norovirus is a small, nonenveloped RNA virus in the family Caliciviridae. **Without a lipid envelope, it resists alcohols, detergents, and drying**, and its low infectious dose lets it spread rapidly in hospitals.

whyNot.0: Norovirus has a single-stranded RNA genome, and genome type is not what decides alcohol resistance.
whyNot.1: Viruses do not form spores; spores are why alcohol fails against Clostridioides difficile.
whyNot.3: Reverse transcriptase is a feature of retroviruses such as HIV, which are enveloped and easily inactivated by alcohol.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., virology chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., viruses chapter (caliciviruses)

items.stem: A patient has a cluster of fresh genital vesicles, and herpes simplex virus is suspected. Which specimen gives the best yield for viral culture or PCR?
options: A swab of the surface of a dry, crusted lesion
Serum collected the same day for HSV IgM
A swab of the intact skin next to the lesions
Fluid and cells from a freshly unroofed vesicle
items.why: Virus is most abundant in early vesicles. **The vesicle is unroofed and its base is swabbed firmly** with a synthetic swab to collect fluid and infected cells, and the swab is placed in viral transport medium.

whyNot.0: Crusted lesions are older and contain much less virus than fresh vesicles.
whyNot.1: Serum is used for serology, not for culture or PCR of the lesion, and IgM may not be present early.
whyNot.2: Intact skin next to the lesions contains little or no virus.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., virology chapter (specimen collection); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., viruses chapter (specimen collection)

items.stem: Scrapings from the base of a skin vesicle are stained with Giemsa (Tzanck smear) and show multinucleated giant cells with molded nuclei. What can be concluded?
options: Herpes simplex or varicella-zoster virus, which this test cannot tell apart
Herpes simplex virus type 2 specifically, since only it forms giant cells
Cytomegalovirus, since its infected cells are multinucleated
Molluscum contagiosum virus, since it also forms vesicles
items.why: The Tzanck smear detects the cytopathic effect of the alphaherpesviruses. **Multinucleated giant cells are seen in both HSV and VZV infections**, so PCR or a direct fluorescent antibody test is needed to name the virus.

whyNot.1: Both HSV types and VZV produce multinucleated giant cells, so the smear cannot identify HSV-2.
whyNot.2: CMV produces enlarged cells with owl's-eye inclusions, and it does not usually cause these vesicles.
whyNot.3: Molluscum causes firm, umbilicated papules with large cytoplasmic inclusion bodies, not giant cells.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., virology chapter (cytology); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., viruses chapter (herpesviruses)

items.stem: In a real-time PCR assay, specimen A has a cycle threshold (Ct) of 18 and specimen B has a Ct of 32 for the same target. Assuming both runs are valid, what does this indicate?
options: Specimen B contained more target, since it went through more cycles
Specimen A contained more target, since it crossed the threshold earlier
Both contained equal target, since Ct reflects only amplification efficiency
Only specimen B is positive, since a positive result needs a Ct above 30
items.why: Product roughly doubles each cycle, so **a lower Ct means more starting target**. A difference of 14 cycles corresponds to roughly 2^14, or about 16,000-fold, more template in specimen A if efficiency were 100%.

whyNot.0: Ct is the cycle at which fluorescence first crosses the threshold; a later Ct means less starting target.
whyNot.2: Ct depends mainly on the amount of starting template when efficiency is similar, as it is for the same assay.
whyNot.3: Higher Ct values mean less target, not a stronger positive; cutoffs are set by each assay, and a low Ct is a strong positive.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., molecular diagnostics chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., nucleic acid-based analytic methods chapter

items.stem: A laboratory identifies bacterial colonies by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry. What does the instrument compare against its reference database?
options: The sequence of the 16S rRNA gene
A pattern of biochemical reactions read by color change
A profile of cellular fatty acids from gas chromatography
A spectrum made up mostly of ribosomal protein masses
items.why: The colony is mixed with a matrix and hit with a laser, which ionizes its proteins; time of flight to the detector reflects the mass-to-charge ratio. **The spectrum, dominated by abundant ribosomal proteins**, is matched to reference spectra. Some closely related organisms, such as E. coli and Shigella, cannot be separated this way.

whyNot.0: 16S rRNA sequencing is a separate molecular method; MALDI-TOF measures proteins, not nucleic acid sequences.
whyNot.1: This describes automated biochemical identification systems, not mass spectrometry.
whyNot.2: Fatty acid profiling by gas chromatography is a different, older identification method.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., automation and molecular methods chapters; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., MALDI-TOF identification section

items.stem: Which pair of organisms is appropriate as the positive and negative controls, respectively, for the cytochrome oxidase test?
items.why: Oxidase-positive organisms such as P. aeruginosa turn the reagent dark purple within seconds, while Enterobacterales such as E. coli do not. **Each new lot of reagent is checked with a known positive and a known negative organism** before patient results are reported.

whyNot.0: These are the right organisms in the wrong roles; E. coli is oxidase negative.
whyNot.1: This pair is used to control the catalase test, not the oxidase test.
whyNot.3: Both are Enterobacterales and are oxidase negative, so neither can serve as a positive control.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., quality in the clinical microbiology laboratory chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., quality control chapter

items.stem: A blood culture bottle flags positive, and the Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. What should the technologist do first?
options: Phone the result to the caregiver, have it read back, and document the call
Wait for the final identification and susceptibility before reporting
Post the result in the information system and rely on the physician to see it
Withhold the result, since cocci in clusters are probably skin contaminants
items.why: A positive blood culture Gram stain is a critical (panic) value. **It is called to a responsible caregiver at once, with read-back and documentation** of who received it and when. This is a postanalytical quality assurance practice.

whyNot.1: Delaying the report holds back information needed for prompt therapy; Gram stain results are reported at once.
whyNot.2: A positive blood culture is a critical value that needs active, direct notification, not passive posting.
whyNot.3: Clusters may be S. aureus; deciding whether an isolate is a contaminant needs identification and clinical correlation, not withholding the report.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., quality in the clinical microbiology laboratory chapter; Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., quality in the clinical microbiology laboratory chapter

items.stem: A laboratory plans to grow Mycobacterium tuberculosis cultures for drug susceptibility testing. Which biosafety level is required for this work?
options: BSL-1: open bench work with standard microbiological practices
BSL-2: open bench work allowed if staff wear surgical masks
BSL-3: inward directional airflow and all open work in a BSC
BSL-4: full-body positive-pressure suits and a separate building
items.why: M. tuberculosis spreads by aerosols and has a low infectious dose. **Propagating and manipulating its cultures requires BSL-3**: controlled access, directional inward airflow, and all open work in a biological safety cabinet. Smears of clinical specimens may be prepared at BSL-2 in a BSC.

whyNot.0: BSL-1 is for well-characterized agents that do not cause disease in healthy adults.
whyNot.1: Surgical masks do not protect against infectious aerosols, and culture work with M. tuberculosis is not done on an open bench.
whyNot.3: BSL-4 is reserved for agents such as Ebola virus that cause life-threatening disease with no available treatment.

items.ref: CDC/NIH, Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL), 6th ed.; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., laboratory safety chapter

items.stem: A stool wet mount shows an elongated, yellow-brown egg up to about 90 µm long, with a thin shell, a thin and irregular mammillated coat, and an interior filled with disorganized refractile granules. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Unfertilized eggs are laid by female worms without males. **They are elongated, thin-shelled, and packed with refractile granules**, and they never embryonate. They are still reported as A. lumbricoides because they show intestinal infection.

whyNot.0: Fertilized eggs are rounder and smaller, with a thick shell and a single undivided cell inside.
whyNot.2: Hookworm eggs are thin-shelled ovals without a mammillated coat and contain a cleaving embryo with a clear space under the shell.
whyNot.3: F. buski eggs are much larger and have an operculum, which this egg lacks.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Ascaris lumbricoides chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Ascariasis

items.stem: Several people develop fever, muscle pain, swelling around the eyes, and marked eosinophilia 1–2 weeks after eating undercooked wild pig meat. A muscle biopsy is done. What is expected to be seen?
options: Fluid-filled cysticerci with an invaginated scolex
Crescent-shaped bradyzoites packed in a tissue cyst
Sheathed microfilariae in the muscle capillaries
Coiled larvae within nurse cells in skeletal muscle
items.why: Trichinellosis follows eating undercooked pork or wild game containing Trichinella larvae. Newborn larvae spread to striated muscle, where **coiled larvae lie within nurse cells**, causing myositis, periorbital edema, and eosinophilia.

whyNot.0: Cysticerci are the larval stage of Taenia solium, acquired by swallowing eggs rather than by eating meat with larvae.
whyNot.1: Tissue cysts with bradyzoites are seen with Toxoplasma or Sarcocystis, which do not produce marked eosinophilia with periorbital edema.
whyNot.2: Microfilariae of filarial worms circulate in blood and are not encysted in muscle.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Trichinella spiralis chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Trichinellosis

items.stem: A stool concentrate from a child shows round eggs about 30–47 µm across with a thin outer shell and a six-hooked oncosphere. Thread-like filaments arise from two polar thickenings of the inner membrane and extend into the space between the oncosphere and the shell. Which cestode is it?
items.why: **Polar filaments in the space between the oncosphere and the outer shell** distinguish H. nana, the dwarf tapeworm, from H. diminuta. H. nana can complete its life cycle in one host, so autoinfection can build up heavy worm burdens in children.

whyNot.1: H. diminuta eggs are larger, about 70–86 µm, and have no polar filaments.
whyNot.2: Taenia eggs have a thick, radially striated shell and no polar filaments.
whyNot.3: Dipylidium eggs are passed in packets enclosed in a membrane, and single eggs lack polar filaments.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Hymenolepis chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Hymenolepiasis

items.stem: A saline wet mount of vaginal discharge shows pear-shaped flagellates about 10–20 µm long with jerky motility and an undulating membrane extending about halfway down the body. Which organism is it?
items.why: T. vaginalis has only a trophozoite stage and is identified in fresh wet mounts by its motility. **Its undulating membrane extends only about half the body length**. Mounts should be examined promptly because the organisms lose motility as the specimen cools.

whyNot.0: Giardia is an intestinal flagellate with two nuclei and a sucking disk; it is not found in vaginal discharge.
whyNot.2: P. hominis is an intestinal flagellate whose undulating membrane runs the full length of the body.
whyNot.3: Chilomastix is an intestinal flagellate with a spiral groove and no undulating membrane.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Trichomonas vaginalis chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Trichomoniasis

items.stem: An iodine-stained stool concentrate shows spherical cysts about 15–25 µm across with up to eight nuclei, each with an eccentric karyosome. Some cysts contain chromatoid bodies with splintered ends. How should this finding be interpreted?
options: Entamoeba histolytica/E. dispar, which needs further testing
Iodamoeba bütschlii, a nonpathogen with a glycogen vacuole
Endolimax nana, a nonpathogen with four small nuclei
Entamoeba coli, a nonpathogen that shows fecal exposure
items.why: **Cysts with up to eight nuclei, eccentric karyosomes, and splinter-like chromatoid bodies** identify Entamoeba coli. It causes no disease but is reported, because it shows the patient swallowed fecally contaminated food or water and may carry pathogens too.

whyNot.0: E. histolytica/E. dispar cysts have no more than four nuclei with central karyosomes, and their chromatoid bodies have smooth, rounded ends.
whyNot.1: Iodamoeba cysts have a single nucleus and a large glycogen vacuole that stains dark with iodine.
whyNot.2: Endolimax cysts are smaller, with up to four nuclei with large blot-like karyosomes and no peripheral chromatin.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., intestinal amoebae chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Intestinal (non-pathogenic) amebae

items.stem: A Giemsa-stained thin blood film shows infected red cells that are normal or slightly small in size, with no Schüffner's dots. Some trophozoites stretch across the cell as a band, and mature schizonts hold about 6–12 merozoites arranged in a rosette around central pigment. Which species is most likely?
items.why: P. malariae infects older red cells and does not enlarge them. **Band-form trophozoites and rosette schizonts with 6–12 merozoites** are characteristic. P. knowlesi, found in Palawan, can look the same on smears, so PCR is needed in areas where it occurs.

whyNot.0: P. vivax enlarges the red cell, shows Schüffner's dots, and its schizonts usually hold 12–24 merozoites.
whyNot.1: P. ovale enlarges the red cell, which is often oval with fringed edges and shows Schüffner's dots.
whyNot.3: P. falciparum schizonts are rarely seen in peripheral blood, and its gametocytes are crescent-shaped.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Plasmodium chapter; CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Malaria

items.stem: Thick and thin blood films are prepared for malaria diagnosis. What is the main advantage of the thick film?
options: It examines more blood, so it is more sensitive for finding parasites
It keeps red cells intact, so species identification is easier
It is fixed with methanol, so red cells are not lysed during staining
It lets parasitemia be reported as a percentage of infected red cells
items.why: The thick film is unfixed, so red cells lyse during staining and parasites from a much larger volume of blood are seen in each field. **This makes the thick film the more sensitive screening film**, while the thin film is used to identify the species.

whyNot.1: This describes the thin film; in the thick film red cells are lysed, so their size and stippling cannot be judged.
whyNot.2: The thin film is fixed with methanol; the thick film is left unfixed so the hemoglobin washes out.
whyNot.3: Percent parasitemia is counted on the thin film; on the thick film parasites are counted against white cells.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Plasmodium chapter (laboratory diagnosis); CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Diagnostic procedures: blood specimens

items.stem: A watery stool is sent without preservative for ova and parasite examination, mainly to look for amoebic trophozoites. Within what time after passage should it be examined?
items.why: Liquid stools are most likely to contain trophozoites, which lose motility and break down quickly. **Liquid specimens should be examined within 30 minutes of passage**, or placed at once into preservatives such as formalin and PVA.

whyNot.0: One hour is the usual limit for soft (semiformed) stool; trophozoites in watery stool degenerate faster.
whyNot.1: This applies to formed stool, which mainly contains cysts; trophozoites in liquid stool do not survive this long.
whyNot.2: Trophozoites break down within hours, so an unpreserved stool held this long is unsuitable.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., parasitology chapter (specimen collection and transport); Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 16th ed., laboratory methods for diagnosis of parasitic infections chapter

items.stem: Before Giemsa-staining malaria films, the buffered water used to dilute the stain is checked with a pH meter against a target of pH 7.2. Why is this an important quality control step?
options: The pH affects only staining speed, so it is checked to set the time
An off-target pH can hide stippling and other parasite details
An acidic buffer lyses the red cells in the fixed thin film
An alkaline buffer is needed to dissolve the malaria pigment
items.why: Giemsa staining is pH dependent. If the buffer is too acidic, films stain too pink and **Schüffner's dots may not appear**, and if it is too alkaline, they stain too blue. Either way parasites can be missed or misidentified, so the buffer pH is checked and recorded.

whyNot.0: The pH changes the colors and the detail that can be seen, not just how fast the stain works.
whyNot.2: Methanol fixation keeps thin-film red cells intact; lysis in the thick film comes from the water, not from pH.
whyNot.3: Pigment is a helpful diagnostic feature, and the buffer is not used to remove it.

items.ref: CDC DPDx (cdc.gov/dpdx), Diagnostic procedures: blood specimens (Giemsa staining); Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., Plasmodium chapter (laboratory diagnosis)

items.stem: A medical ward sends four specimens to the microbiology laboratory, each labelled for routine bacterial culture. Which one should be declined, with a request for a more suitable specimen?
options: Pleural fluid aspirated into a sterile tube
Bone fragment from debridement in a sterile container
Tip of a Foley urinary catheter removed from a febrile patient
Purulent material from deep in a surgical wound
items.why: A Foley catheter tip is coated with urethral and periurethral flora as it is pulled out, so whatever grows cannot be linked to infection. **Foley catheter tips are unacceptable for culture**; urine should instead be aspirated from the disinfected sampling port of the catheter.

whyNot.0: Pleural fluid comes from a normally sterile site and, collected by aspiration into a sterile container, is an acceptable specimen.
whyNot.1: Bone or tissue from debridement is one of the best specimens for osteomyelitis and is accepted for culture.
whyNot.3: Pus collected from deep in a wound is acceptable; aspirates or tissue are preferred over surface swabs, but the specimen is not rejected.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, specimen collection and processing chapter (rejection criteria); Bailey & Scott 16e, specimen management chapter

items.stem: A clean-catch urine is streaked with a 0.001-mL calibrated loop onto a sheep blood agar plate. After overnight incubation, 42 colonies of one gram-negative bacillus are counted. What colony count should be reported?
items.why: Each colony represents one colony-forming unit in the volume plated, so the count is divided by that volume in mL. With a 0.001-mL loop, **CFU/mL = number of colonies × 1,000**, giving 42 × 1,000 = 42,000 (4.2 × 10^4) CFU/mL.

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 10, which would apply only if 0.1 mL had been plated.
whyNot.1: This multiplies by 100, the factor for a 0.01-mL loop, not a 0.001-mL loop.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 10,000, as if only 0.0001 mL had been plated.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, urinary tract infections chapter (quantitative urine culture); Bailey & Scott 16e, urinary tract infections chapter

worked.problem: A urine is plated with a 0.01-mL calibrated loop and 37 colonies grow. What is the colony count?
steps: Volume plated = 0.01 mL, so the multiplication factor is 1 ÷ 0.01 = 100.

items.stem: A stool culture is plated on Hektoen enteric (HE) agar. After overnight incubation, one colony type is green to blue-green with no black center, and the surrounding medium is unchanged. Which organism best fits this appearance?
items.why: HE agar uses bile salts to inhibit gram-positive bacteria, and lactose, sucrose and salicin with bromthymol blue and acid fuchsin to show fermentation; ferric ammonium citrate with thiosulfate detects H2S. **Organisms that ferment none of these sugars and make no H2S, typically Shigella, form green colonies without black centers.**

whyNot.0: Enterobacter ferments lactose and sucrose, so its colonies are yellow-orange (salmon) on HE agar.
whyNot.2: Most Salmonella produce H2S, giving blue-green colonies with black centers.
whyNot.3: Proteus mirabilis usually produces H2S, so its colonies often have black centers.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Enterobacterales chapter (selective and differential media); Bailey & Scott 16e, Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: A teenager has fever and right lower abdominal pain that mimics appendicitis after eating undercooked pork. Stool plated on cefsulodin-irgasan-novobiocin (CIN) agar and incubated at 25–30 °C shows colonies with a deep red center and a clear outer zone at 48 hours. Which test best separates the suspected pathogen from Aeromonas, which can look the same on this medium?
items.why: CIN agar is selective for Yersinia enterocolitica, whose mannitol fermentation with a neutral red indicator gives a 'bull's-eye' colony after 48 hours at 25–30 °C. Aeromonas can form a similar colony, but **Yersinia is oxidase negative whereas Aeromonas is oxidase positive**, so an oxidase test on the colony quickly separates them.

whyNot.0: Y. enterocolitica is usually a non-lactose fermenter and Aeromonas is variable, so lactose fermentation does not reliably separate them.
whyNot.1: Both organisms are gram-negative bacilli, so the Gram stain cannot tell them apart.
whyNot.2: Both ferment glucose and give an acid butt in TSI.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Enterobacterales chapter (Yersinia) and Vibrio/Aeromonas chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: A blood culture grows catalase-positive, gram-positive cocci in clusters. A slide coagulase (clumping factor) test on a colony from sheep blood agar is negative. What should be done before reporting the isolate as a coagulase-negative staphylococcus?
options: Do a tube coagulase test, read at 4 h and at 24 h
Repeat the slide test using a heavier inoculum
Do a catalase test using 30% hydrogen peroxide
Report it as CoNS, since the slide test is definitive
items.why: The slide test detects bound coagulase (clumping factor), which some Staphylococcus aureus strains lack, while the tube test detects free coagulase. **A negative slide coagulase test must be confirmed with a tube test**, incubated at 35–37 °C and read at 4 hours and again at 18–24 hours, because some strains clot late and fibrinolysin can dissolve an early clot.

whyNot.1: A heavier inoculum does not create clumping factor in a strain that lacks it, and very heavy suspensions can autoagglutinate.
whyNot.2: The isolate is already known to be catalase positive; 30% hydrogen peroxide (superoxol) is used for Neisseria, not to separate S. aureus.
whyNot.3: A negative slide test is not definitive because some S. aureus lack clumping factor, so the tube test is required.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Staphylococcus chapter (coagulase tests); Bailey & Scott 16e, Staphylococcus chapter

items.stem: An 8-year-old with sore throat, fever and tender anterior neck nodes has a negative rapid group A streptococcal antigen test. Two throat swabs were collected together. What is the recommended next step?
options: Report the result as negative for group A Streptococcus
Repeat the rapid antigen test on the same swab
Culture the second swab on sheep blood agar
Request a heterophile antibody test instead
items.why: Rapid antigen tests are specific but only moderately sensitive, so a negative result can miss true group A streptococcal pharyngitis. **In children and adolescents, a negative rapid antigen test should be backed up by throat culture** (or a sensitive molecular test), because untreated infection carries a risk of rheumatic fever.

whyNot.0: Reporting a final negative ignores the false-negative rate of the rapid test in a child, the group most at risk of complications.
whyNot.1: Repeating the same insensitive test on the same swab does not improve sensitivity.
whyNot.3: A heterophile test looks for infectious mononucleosis; it does not replace backup testing for group A Streptococcus.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Streptococcus chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Streptococcus and upper respiratory tract infections chapters

items.stem: A fish vendor at a wet market has a painful, purplish swelling on the finger that began after a cut from a fish fin. Culture yields a small gram-positive rod with alpha hemolysis. Which result most strongly supports Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae?
options: Tumbling motility in a wet mount at room temperature
Blackening of the butt of a triple sugar iron slant
A positive CAMP reaction with Staphylococcus aureus
items.why: Erysipeloid follows skin injury while handling fish, shellfish, poultry or meat. Erysipelothrix is catalase negative and nonmotile, and **it is the main gram-positive rod that produces H2S in TSI**, which separates it from Listeria, Corynebacterium and lactobacilli.

whyNot.0: Tumbling motility at room temperature is typical of Listeria monocytogenes; Erysipelothrix is nonmotile.
whyNot.2: A positive CAMP reaction suggests Listeria (or group B Streptococcus); Erysipelothrix is CAMP negative.
whyNot.3: Erysipelothrix is catalase negative; a positive catalase points to Listeria or Corynebacterium.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, aerobic gram-positive bacilli chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Erysipelothrix and similar organisms chapter

items.stem: A throat swab from an unvaccinated child with a gray membrane over the tonsils is subcultured to Tinsdale medium. Black colonies surrounded by a brown halo appear after 24–48 hours. What does the brown halo indicate?
items.why: Tinsdale medium contains potassium tellurite and L-cystine; corynebacteria reduce tellurite to form black colonies. **The brown halo comes from cystinase**, which releases H2S from cystine, and is typical of C. diphtheriae and the related C. ulcerans and C. pseudotuberculosis. Toxin production must still be confirmed separately.

whyNot.1: Urease is tested separately (C. diphtheriae is urease negative, C. ulcerans positive) and does not cause the halo.
whyNot.2: Lecithinase is shown on egg yolk agar, for example by Clostridium perfringens.
whyNot.3: Pyrazinamidase is tested separately and is negative in C. diphtheriae; it does not produce a halo.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Corynebacterium chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Corynebacterium and related organisms chapter

items.stem: Within 1–5 hours of a fiesta lunch, many guests develop nausea and vomiting. Leftover fried rice is suspected, and Bacillus cereus emetic toxin is considered. Which specimen best links the outbreak to this source?
options: Blood cultures from the sickest guests
Throat swabs from the kitchen staff
Urine samples from the affected guests
items.why: The emetic form of B. cereus food poisoning is caused by a heat-stable toxin already formed in starchy food, so the organism does not need to grow in the patient or invade. Because B. cereus is common in the environment and can be found in some healthy people's stools, **recovering large numbers (about 10^5 CFU/g or more) from the implicated food** is the best evidence.

whyNot.0: B. cereus food poisoning is a toxin-mediated illness without bacteremia, so blood cultures will not help.
whyNot.1: B. cereus is a soil and food organism, not a throat carrier; throat or nose swabs of food handlers are used for staphylococcal outbreaks.
whyNot.2: The organism is not excreted in urine in food poisoning.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Bacillus chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Bacillus and similar organisms chapter

items.stem: An Enterobacterales isolate is tested in Moeller lysine decarboxylase broth alongside a control tube of the same base without amino acid. Both tubes are overlaid with mineral oil and read after incubation. Which pair of results is a valid positive lysine decarboxylase test?
options: Lysine tube yellow; control tube yellow
Lysine tube purple; control tube yellow
Lysine tube purple; control tube purple
Lysine tube yellow; control tube purple
items.why: The organism first ferments the small amount of glucose, turning the bromcresol purple indicator yellow, and this acid pH activates the decarboxylase. **If lysine is decarboxylated, alkaline cadaverine turns the tube back to purple while the amino acid–free control stays yellow.** The oil overlay keeps the tubes anaerobic so that oxidative alkalinization does not mimic a positive.

whyNot.0: Both tubes yellow means glucose was fermented but lysine was not decarboxylated: a negative result.
whyNot.2: A purple control means the base became alkaline without the amino acid (for example, glucose was not fermented), so the test cannot be interpreted.
whyNot.3: A purple control makes the test invalid, and a yellow lysine tube would be negative anyway.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, biochemical identification of gram-negative bacteria chapter (decarboxylase tests); Bailey & Scott 16e, Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: A known Escherichia coli strain, used as a negative control, gives a purple color within seconds in a filter-paper oxidase test with Kovács oxidase reagent (tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine). Which technique error most likely explains this?
options: Taking the colony from sheep blood agar
Using reagent prepared fresh that morning
Applying the colony with a nichrome wire loop
items.why: The oxidase reagent is turned into a purple compound by cytochrome c oxidase, but iron in nichrome or other metal loops can oxidize it as well. **Colonies should be transferred with a platinum loop or a wooden or plastic stick** to avoid false-positive oxidase reactions.

whyNot.0: Sheep blood agar is a suitable source; colonies from media with fermentable sugars or dyes, such as MacConkey agar, are the ones to avoid.
whyNot.1: Reading within about 10 seconds is correct; color appearing later is not considered positive.
whyNot.2: Fresh reagent is recommended because the reagent oxidizes on standing; it does not cause false positives.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, biochemical identification chapter (oxidase test); Bailey & Scott 16e, biochemical identification of gram-negative bacteria

items.stem: An ICU patient receiving meropenem develops ventilator-associated pneumonia. The tracheal aspirate grows a motile, oxidase-negative, non-glucose-fermenting gram-negative bacillus with lavender-green colonies on blood agar and an ammonia-like odor. It is DNase positive, lysine decarboxylase positive, and oxidizes maltose more strongly than glucose. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: S. maltophilia is a nonfermenter that is usually oxidase negative, motile, DNase positive, lysine decarboxylase positive, and a stronger oxidizer of maltose than glucose. **It is intrinsically resistant to carbapenems through a chromosomal metallo-β-lactamase**, which is why it emerges in patients receiving these drugs; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the usual treatment.

whyNot.0: Acinetobacter is also oxidase negative but is nonmotile and DNase negative.
whyNot.1: Achromobacter xylosoxidans is oxidase positive and oxidizes xylose rather than maltose strongly.
whyNot.2: Elizabethkingia meningoseptica is oxidase positive, nonmotile and indole positive.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia chapter; CLSI M100 (intrinsic resistance)

items.stem: Sputum from a teenager with cystic fibrosis is plated for routine culture. Which medium is added specifically to recover Burkholderia cepacia complex from the heavy mixed flora?
items.why: In cystic fibrosis, mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus can overgrow other organisms, and B. cepacia complex infection has major prognostic and infection-control importance. **Selective media such as BCSA, OFPBL or PC agar**, which contain polymyxin and other inhibitors, are used so that B. cepacia complex is not missed.

whyNot.1: CIN agar is used to isolate Yersinia enterocolitica from stool.
whyNot.2: TCBS agar is used to isolate Vibrio species from stool.
whyNot.3: BCYE agar is used to grow Legionella.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli chapter (Burkholderia); Bailey & Scott 16e, Burkholderia cepacia complex chapter

items.stem: A Gram-stained vaginal smear is scored by the Nugent method. Which combination of morphotypes gives a score in the bacterial vaginosis range (7–10)?
options: Many large gram-positive rods; no small gram-variable rods
Many large gram-positive rods; many budding yeast cells
No large gram-positive rods; many small gram-variable rods
items.why: The Nugent score adds points for loss of Lactobacillus morphotypes (large gram-positive rods), for an excess of Gardnerella/Bacteroides morphotypes (small gram-variable rods), and for curved Mobiluncus morphotypes. **Absent lactobacilli with many small gram-variable rods scores 7–10, consistent with bacterial vaginosis**; clue cells are the matching wet-mount finding.

whyNot.0: A Lactobacillus-dominant smear scores 0–3, which is normal flora.
whyNot.1: Yeasts are not scored by the Nugent method; with many lactobacilli this suggests candidiasis, not bacterial vaginosis.
whyNot.3: These findings suggest gonorrhea, which the Nugent score does not assess.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, genital tract infections chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, genital tract infections chapter (Nugent scoring)

items.stem: For broth microdilution, a bacterial suspension is adjusted to a 0.5 McFarland standard, taken as about 1.5 × 10^8 CFU/mL. The final concentration needed in each well is 5 × 10^5 CFU/mL. What overall dilution of the standardized suspension is required?
items.why: The dilution factor is the starting concentration divided by the target: 1.5 × 10^8 ÷ 5 × 10^5 = 300. **An overall 1:300 dilution gives about 5 × 10^5 CFU/mL**, the inoculum specified for broth microdilution; a heavier inoculum falsely raises MICs and a lighter one lowers them.

whyNot.0: A 1:30 dilution gives 5 × 10^6 CFU/mL, ten times too heavy.
whyNot.1: A 1:150 dilution gives 1 × 10^6 CFU/mL, twice the target.
whyNot.3: A 1:3,000 dilution gives 5 × 10^4 CFU/mL, ten times too light.

items.ref: CLSI M07 and M100 (inoculum standardization); Mahon & Lehman 7e, antimicrobial susceptibility testing chapter

worked.problem: A 0.5 McFarland suspension (about 1.5 × 10^8 CFU/mL) must be diluted to 1 × 10^6 CFU/mL. What dilution is needed?
steps: Dilution factor = starting concentration ÷ target concentration.

items.stem: A lung abscess aspirate grows an anaerobic gram-negative bacillus with thin, pointed ends. Special-potency disks are placed on the primary anaerobic blood agar plate. Which pattern (vancomycin 5 µg / kanamycin 1 mg / colistin 10 µg) is expected for Fusobacterium nucleatum?
items.why: Gram-negative anaerobes are almost always vancomycin resistant, and kanamycin and colistin then separate the genera. **Fusobacterium is resistant to vancomycin but susceptible to kanamycin and colistin**, whereas the Bacteroides fragilis group is resistant to all three disks.

whyNot.0: Resistance to all three disks is the pattern of the B. fragilis group.
whyNot.2: Vancomycin susceptible with kanamycin and colistin resistance is the unusual pattern of Porphyromonas.
whyNot.3: Vancomycin and kanamycin susceptible with colistin resistance is typical of gram-positive anaerobes.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, anaerobes chapter (special-potency disks); Bailey & Scott 16e, overview of anaerobic bacteriology chapter

items.stem: An anaerobic isolate is streaked across an egg yolk agar plate, one half of which was first spread with Clostridium perfringens alpha antitoxin. After incubation, an opaque zone forms around growth on the untreated half but not on the antitoxin half. What does this result show?
options: Lecithinase activity neutralized by specific antitoxin
Lipase activity forming an iridescent surface sheen
Proteolysis that clears the egg yolk emulsion
Beta-hemolysis inhibited by the egg yolk proteins
items.why: This is the Nagler reaction. The alpha toxin of C. perfringens is a lecithinase (phospholipase C) that breaks down egg yolk lecithin to form an opaque precipitate in the agar. **Loss of the opacity where alpha antitoxin was applied shows the lecithinase is C. perfringens alpha toxin.**

whyNot.1: Lipase produces an oily, iridescent sheen on the colony surface and is not neutralized by alpha antitoxin.
whyNot.2: Proteolysis clears the medium rather than making it opaque.
whyNot.3: Egg yolk agar does not show hemolysis; the double zone of hemolysis is read on blood agar.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, anaerobes chapter (Clostridium); Bailey & Scott 16e, spore-forming gram-positive anaerobic bacilli chapter

items.stem: After a molar extraction, a farmer develops a hard swelling of the jaw with draining sinus tracts. Yellow granules in the pus are crushed and Gram stained, showing branching gram-positive rods; the modified acid-fast stain is negative. Culture grows best under anaerobic conditions. What is the most likely organism?
items.why: Cervicofacial actinomycosis follows dental trauma or extraction, when oral Actinomyces invade tissue and form 'sulfur granules'. **Branching gram-positive rods that are not acid-fast and grow anaerobically** point to Actinomyces israelii, whose colonies often look like a molar tooth.

whyNot.0: Nocardia is aerobic and partially acid-fast with the modified stain.
whyNot.1: Streptomyces is an aerobic actinomycete that mainly causes mycetoma of the foot.
whyNot.2: C. diphtheriae does not branch, does not form granules, and grows aerobically.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, anaerobes chapter (Actinomyces); Bailey & Scott 16e, Actinomyces and similar organisms chapter

items.stem: A man from a rural province has hypopigmented skin patches with loss of sensation and thickened ulnar nerves, and leprosy (Hansen disease) is suspected. Which laboratory test is used to support the diagnosis?
options: Acid-fast stained slit-skin smears, graded as a bacteriologic index
Culture of a skin biopsy on Löwenstein-Jensen medium
An interferon-gamma release assay on whole blood
A lepromin skin test read at 3–4 weeks
items.why: Mycobacterium leprae has never been grown on artificial media, so the laboratory supports the clinical diagnosis by direct staining. **Slit-skin smears (or skin biopsies) stained for acid-fast bacilli are graded as a bacteriologic index**; because M. leprae is less acid-fast than M. tuberculosis, a weaker acid decolorizer is used, as in the Fite method for tissue.

whyNot.1: M. leprae does not grow on Löwenstein-Jensen or any other artificial medium; it can be propagated only in mouse footpads or armadillos.
whyNot.2: Interferon-gamma release assays are designed to detect M. tuberculosis infection and are not used to diagnose leprosy.
whyNot.3: The lepromin (Mitsuda) test reflects cell-mediated immunity and helps classify the form of leprosy; many unexposed people react, so it does not diagnose infection.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Mycobacterium chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Mycobacteria chapter; WHO Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy

items.stem: Pertussis is suspected in an infant with paroxysmal cough and vomiting after coughing spells. A posterior nasopharyngeal swab is to be collected for culture. Which swab and plating medium should be used?
options: Dacron or flocked swab; Regan-Lowe charcoal agar
Dacron or flocked swab; MacConkey agar
items.why: B. pertussis attaches to the ciliated cells of the nasopharynx and needs special media. **A Dacron, rayon or flocked swab plated on charcoal-containing Regan-Lowe (or Bordet-Gengou) medium** is used, because cotton contains fatty acids that are toxic to the organism; plates are held for up to 7 days, and PCR is now more sensitive than culture.

whyNot.1: The medium is right, but cotton contains fatty acids that are toxic to B. pertussis.
whyNot.2: The swab is right, but B. pertussis does not grow on MacConkey agar.
whyNot.3: Cotton is toxic to B. pertussis, and the organism does not grow on routine sheep blood agar.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Bordetella chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Bordetella pertussis and Bordetella parapertussis chapter

items.stem: A man has an infected wound over his knuckles after punching someone in the mouth. A slow-growing gram-negative bacillus forms small colonies that pit the agar on blood and chocolate agar in CO2, with a bleach-like odor. It does not grow on MacConkey agar and is oxidase positive and catalase negative. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Eikenella corrodens is part of the oral flora, so it is classically recovered from human bites and clenched-fist injuries. **Pitting colonies with a bleach-like odor that are oxidase positive, catalase negative and do not grow on MacConkey agar** identify it; it is also the 'E' of the HACEK endocarditis group.

whyNot.0: Pasteurella comes from cat and dog bites and is catalase and indole positive, without pitting.
whyNot.1: Capnocytophaga canimorsus is linked to dog bites, forms thin fusiform rods, and is catalase and oxidase positive.
whyNot.2: H. parainfluenzae needs V factor, so it does not grow on sheep blood agar alone, and it neither pits the agar nor smells of bleach.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, fastidious gram-negative bacilli chapter (HACEK); Bailey & Scott 16e, Eikenella and related organisms chapter

items.stem: A pregnant woman at a routine prenatal visit has a reactive RPR at a titer of 1:2. She has no lesions and no history of syphilis. A Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TP-PA) test is nonreactive and remains nonreactive on a repeat specimen 4 weeks later. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Prozone effect in the RPR test
Syphilis treated adequately in the past
items.why: RPR and VDRL detect antibodies to a cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol antigen, which can be present in pregnancy, autoimmune disease, some infections and other conditions. **A reactive nontreponemal test with a repeatedly nonreactive treponemal test is a biologic false positive**, so syphilis is not diagnosed.

whyNot.0: Latent syphilis would give a reactive treponemal test such as TP-PA.
whyNot.1: Prozone causes a falsely negative or weak reaction in undiluted serum with very high antibody levels, not a low-titer reactive RPR.
whyNot.3: After treated syphilis, treponemal tests usually stay reactive for life, so a nonreactive TP-PA argues against past infection.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, spirochetes chapter (syphilis serology); Bailey & Scott 16e, Treponema, Borrelia and Leptospira chapter

items.stem: A patient with advanced HIV has headache and fever. The CSF India ink preparation shows no encapsulated yeasts. Which test on the CSF is most sensitive for cryptococcal meningitis?
options: Repeat India ink on a larger centrifuged volume
Cryptococcal antigen detection by lateral flow assay
Gram stain of the cytocentrifuged sediment
Germ tube test on the CSF sediment
items.why: India ink shows the capsule under the microscope but misses many cases, especially when few yeasts are present. **Detecting capsular polysaccharide (glucuronoxylomannan) by lateral flow assay or latex agglutination is far more sensitive**, and fungal culture should also be set up.

whyNot.0: Repeating India ink is still microscopy with limited sensitivity.
whyNot.2: Gram stain shows yeasts poorly and is less sensitive than India ink.
whyNot.3: The germ tube test identifies Candida albicans colonies; it is not a test for cryptococcal meningitis.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, opportunistic mycoses chapter (Cryptococcus); Bailey & Scott 16e, laboratory methods in mycology / yeasts chapter

items.stem: A gardener pricked by a rose thorn develops a chain of nodules that ulcerate along the lymphatics of the forearm. At 25 °C, culture grows a mold with thin septate hyphae and small conidia clustered like petals at the tips of slender conidiophores. At 37 °C, it converts to small, elongated (cigar-shaped) budding yeasts. Which fungus is it?
items.why: Nodules spreading along lymphatics after a thorn or plant injury are classic for sporotrichosis. **Sporothrix schenckii is thermally dimorphic, forming a mold with 'flowerette' conidia at 25 °C and cigar-shaped yeasts at 37 °C.**

whyNot.1: Talaromyces (formerly Penicillium) marneffei forms a mold with a diffusible red pigment and brush-like conidiophores at 25 °C, and yeasts that divide by fission (with a cross wall) at 37 °C.
whyNot.2: Paracoccidioides forms a slow-growing mold at 25 °C and, at 37 °C, large yeasts with multiple narrow-based buds (a 'mariner's wheel').
whyNot.3: Fonsecaea is a dematiaceous mold causing chromoblastomycosis; it forms sclerotic bodies in tissue, not cigar-shaped yeasts.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, subcutaneous mycoses chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, thermally dimorphic fungi chapter

items.stem: A patient with advanced HIV has fever, dry cough and diffuse bilateral lung infiltrates, and Pneumocystis pneumonia is suspected. Induced sputum is sent to the laboratory. Which approach can confirm the diagnosis?
options: Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar for up to 4 weeks
Serum cryptococcal antigen by lateral flow assay
Immunofluorescent staining or PCR of the specimen
Blood culture in a lysis-centrifugation tube
items.why: Pneumocystis jirovecii cannot be grown in routine culture, so it must be found directly in respiratory specimens. **Immunofluorescent antibody staining (or GMS, calcofluor white or Giemsa-type stains) and PCR** are used; GMS shows round to cup-shaped cysts about 4–7 µm across, and bronchoalveolar lavage is more sensitive than induced sputum.

whyNot.0: P. jirovecii does not grow on fungal culture media, however long they are incubated.
whyNot.1: Cryptococcal antigen testing detects Cryptococcus, not Pneumocystis.
whyNot.3: Lysis-centrifugation blood cultures help recover Histoplasma and other fungi from blood; Pneumocystis is not recovered in culture.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, opportunistic mycoses chapter (Pneumocystis); Bailey & Scott 16e, Pneumocystis jirovecii chapter

items.stem: During the rainy season, a 6-year-old has fever, headache and neck stiffness. The CSF shows a mildly raised white count with mostly lymphocytes, normal glucose, and a negative Gram stain. Which test is best for confirming the most common viral cause?
options: Viral culture of CSF in monkey kidney cells
Serum IgM antibody to herpes simplex virus
Bacterial culture of CSF on chocolate agar
items.why: These findings fit aseptic (viral) meningitis, which in children is caused mostly by enteroviruses. **RT-PCR of CSF is the most sensitive and fastest test for enteroviral meningitis**, and a positive result can shorten antibiotic use and hospital stay.

whyNot.0: Cell culture is slower and less sensitive, and some enteroviruses grow poorly or not at all.
whyNot.1: Serum HSV IgM is not useful for diagnosing acute CNS infection; HSV is detected by CSF PCR, and it is a less common cause here.
whyNot.2: Bacterial culture helps exclude bacterial meningitis but cannot detect a virus.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, viral pathogens chapter (enteroviruses) and CNS infections chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, laboratory diagnosis of viral infections chapter

items.stem: Fluid from a cluster of vesicles on a patient's lip is inoculated into human fibroblast (MRC-5) and A549 cell cultures. If herpes simplex virus is present, which cytopathic effect is expected?
options: Enlarged, rounded, refractile cells within 1–3 days, spreading quickly
Small foci of swollen cells in fibroblasts only, enlarging over 1–3 weeks
Large syncytia forming mainly in HEp-2 cells
Grapelike clusters of rounded cells, best seen in A549 cells
items.why: Herpes simplex virus grows in many cell types and replicates quickly. **Rounding and ballooning of cells that appear within 1–3 days and spread rapidly across the monolayer** is typical of HSV, whereas cytomegalovirus and varicella-zoster virus produce slow, focal CPE.

whyNot.1: Slow, focal CPE limited to fibroblasts and developing over 1–3 weeks is the pattern of cytomegalovirus.
whyNot.2: Syncytia in HEp-2 cells are typical of respiratory syncytial virus.
whyNot.3: Grapelike clusters of rounded cells in A549 or HEp-2 cells are typical of adenovirus.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, laboratory diagnosis of viral infections chapter (cell culture); Bailey & Scott 16e, laboratory methods in virology chapter

items.stem: A 10-month-old in a crowded ward has vomiting followed by profuse watery diarrhea, and rotavirus is suspected. Which specimen and test are most appropriate?
options: Rectal swab for culture on TCBS agar
items.why: Rotavirus is shed in very large amounts in stool early in illness and grows poorly in routine cell culture. **Stool tested by enzyme immunoassay, a rapid antigen test or PCR** is the standard approach; stool should be collected early and refrigerated if testing is delayed.

whyNot.0: Rotavirus is an enteric virus and is not looked for in respiratory specimens; it also grows poorly in routine culture.
whyNot.2: Serology is not used for diagnosing acute rotavirus infection.
whyNot.3: TCBS agar isolates Vibrio species and cannot detect a virus.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, viral pathogens chapter (rotavirus); Bailey & Scott 16e, laboratory diagnosis of viral infections chapter

items.stem: Brain tissue from a patient with suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease was processed in the laboratory. Which method is recommended for decontaminating reusable, heat-resistant instruments that touched the tissue?
options: A standard autoclave cycle at 121 °C for 15 minutes
Immersion in 1 N sodium hydroxide, then extended autoclaving
items.why: Prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid and resist the usual heat, radiation and chemical treatments. **Combined treatment with 1 N sodium hydroxide (or strong hypochlorite) and extended or high-temperature autoclaving** is recommended, and disposable items should be incinerated.

whyNot.0: A routine 15-minute cycle at 121 °C does not reliably inactivate prions.
whyNot.1: Formalin does not inactivate prions and can stabilize their infectivity.
whyNot.3: Glutaraldehyde, like other aldehydes, does not inactivate prions and may fix them onto instruments.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, control of microorganisms chapter (prions); Bailey & Scott 16e, laboratory safety and sterilization chapter; WHO infection control guidelines for transmissible spongiform encephalopathies

items.stem: An anaerobic jar with a gas-generating sachet is set up with a methylene blue indicator strip. After the time recommended by the manufacturer, the strip is still blue. What does this mean?
options: Anaerobic conditions have not been reached
The carbon dioxide level is too high for anaerobes
The strip has detected hydrogen gas in the jar
items.why: Methylene blue is blue when oxidized and becomes colorless when reduced. **A strip that stays blue means oxygen is still present**, so the jar seal, the sachet or the catalyst should be checked and the plates moved to a working system.

whyNot.0: Anaerobiosis would turn the methylene blue strip colorless.
whyNot.2: The indicator responds to the oxidation-reduction state, not to carbon dioxide.
whyNot.3: The strip does not detect hydrogen; it shows whether oxygen has been removed.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, anaerobes chapter (anaerobic incubation systems); Bailey & Scott 16e, anaerobic bacteriology chapter

items.stem: On a daily Gram stain quality-control slide made from Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, both organisms appear purple. What is the most likely cause?
options: Safranin was left on too long
items.why: Decolorization is the critical step: it removes the crystal violet–iodine complex from gram-negative cells but not from gram-positive cells. **If gram-negative control cells stay purple, the smear was under-decolorized** (or was too thick), so patient smears from that run should be reviewed.

whyNot.0: Leaving the counterstain on longer does not make gram-negative cells purple.
whyNot.1: Without iodine, crystal violet washes out of gram-positive cells too, so both organisms would look pink.
whyNot.2: Over-decolorization makes gram-positive cells look pink, not gram-negative cells purple.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, microscopy chapter (Gram stain and quality control); Bailey & Scott 16e, role of microscopy chapter

items.stem: During weekly disk diffusion QC with E. coli ATCC 25922, the zones for amoxicillin-clavulanate and imipenem are below their acceptable ranges, while all other agents on the same plates are in range. The disk cartridges had been kept in the refrigerator door and opened while still cold. What is the most likely cause?
options: Loss of potency of the labile disks during storage
An inoculum heavier than the 0.5 McFarland standard
Agar poured deeper than the standard 4 mm
Contamination of the QC strain with another organism
items.why: Inoculum density and agar depth affect every drug on the plate, so an error limited to a few agents points to the disks. **Clavulanate combinations and carbapenems are among the most labile agents**, and condensation from opening cold cartridges speeds their breakdown; working disks should be kept refrigerated with desiccant and allowed to reach room temperature before opening.

whyNot.1: A heavy inoculum would shrink the zones of all agents, not just two.
whyNot.2: Agar that is too deep would make all zones smaller, not just two.
whyNot.3: A mixed culture would usually show up on a purity plate and would affect more than two agents.

items.ref: CLSI M02 and M100 (disk storage and QC troubleshooting); Mahon & Lehman 7e, antimicrobial susceptibility testing chapter

items.stem: Oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococci grow on modified Thayer-Martin agar from a vaginal swab of a 5-year-old girl. What should the laboratory do before reporting Neisseria gonorrhoeae?
options: Report it presumptively, as colony and Gram stain are typical
Confirm the identification by two tests with different principles
Do a beta-lactamase test and report if it is positive
Discard the isolate once the presumptive report is sent
items.why: In a child, gonococcal infection implies sexual abuse and carries legal consequences, while commensal Neisseria species and Moraxella can be mistaken for N. gonorrhoeae. **The identification must be confirmed by at least two methods based on different principles** (for example, biochemical and MALDI-TOF or molecular), and the isolate should be saved.

whyNot.0: A presumptive identification is not acceptable when a misidentification would have serious legal and social consequences.
whyNot.2: Beta-lactamase production is a resistance property; it does not confirm the species.
whyNot.3: The isolate should be kept for confirmation and possible further testing, not discarded.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Neisseria and Moraxella chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Neisseria chapter; CDC STI Treatment Guidelines (sexual assault and abuse in children)

items.stem: A TB culture laboratory decontaminates sputum with NALC-NaOH. Over the last quarter, only 0.5% of cultures were lost to contamination, against a commonly used target of about 2–5%, and the rate of smear-positive, culture-negative specimens has risen. What is the most likely problem?
options: Specimens are being refrigerated too long before processing
The NALC is liquefying the mucus too efficiently
Too little NaOH is being used, so normal flora survive
Decontamination is too harsh and is killing mycobacteria
items.why: Every decontamination step kills some mycobacteria along with the normal flora, so a small proportion of contaminated cultures is expected. **A contamination rate below about 2%, together with more smear-positive, culture-negative specimens, suggests the decontamination is too harsh**, for example NaOH that is too concentrated or left on too long.

whyNot.0: Delays before processing let normal flora multiply and would raise, not lower, the contamination rate.
whyNot.1: NALC is only a mucolytic agent; it does not kill mycobacteria.
whyNot.2: Too little NaOH would push the contamination rate above the target range.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Mycobacterium chapter (specimen processing and quality control); Bailey & Scott 16e, Mycobacteria chapter

items.stem: A hospital laboratory is sending whole blood from a patient with suspected dengue to a reference laboratory for PCR by courier. Which shipping classification applies?
options: UN 2814, Infectious substance affecting humans (Category A)
Exempt human specimen (minimal likelihood of pathogens)
items.why: Patient specimens sent for diagnosis that are not expected to contain a Category A agent are shipped as **UN 3373, 'Biological substance, Category B', in triple packaging**. Category A (UN 2814) is reserved for agents that can cause permanent disability or death in healthy people on exposure, such as Ebola virus or cultures of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

whyNot.0: Only cultures of dengue virus fall under Category A; a patient specimen sent for diagnosis is Category B.
whyNot.1: UN 3291 covers clinical waste for disposal, not diagnostic specimens.
whyNot.2: The exempt category is for specimens with minimal likelihood of pathogens; a specimen sent for dengue PCR is expected to contain one.

items.ref: WHO Guidance on regulations for the transport of infectious substances; Mahon & Lehman 7e, laboratory safety chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, specimen management chapter (packaging and shipping)

items.stem: A blood culture from a farmer who drinks raw goat's milk grows tiny, faintly staining gram-negative coccobacilli after 4 days. They are oxidase positive and urease positive and do not grow on MacConkey agar. What should the technologist do next?
options: Do all further work in a biosafety cabinet
Sniff the plates to check for an odor
Run a biochemical ID panel on the open bench
Subculture to more media on the open bench
items.why: Brucella is one of the most common causes of laboratory-acquired infection because it spreads by aerosols and has a very low infectious dose. **When Brucella is suspected, all further work should be done in a biosafety cabinet with BSL-3 practices**, plates should never be sniffed, and the isolate should be referred to a reference laboratory for confirmation.

whyNot.1: Sniffing plates has caused laboratory-acquired brucellosis and should never be done.
whyNot.2: Open-bench work creates aerosols, and commercial panels can misidentify Brucella.
whyNot.3: Open-bench subculturing exposes staff to infectious aerosols.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, Brucella chapter and laboratory safety chapter; Bailey & Scott 16e, Brucella chapter; CDC/NIH Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories

items.stem: A 7-year-old from a farming barangay develops cough, wheezing and passing lung infiltrates with marked blood eosinophilia. Stool ova and parasite exams are negative, but Ascaris lumbricoides eggs appear in stool about 2 months later. Why were the early stool exams negative?
options: Stools were examined only by direct wet mount
Adult worms shed eggs only every few weeks
Larvae were still in the lungs, not yet egg-laying adults
The child was reinfected later through the skin
items.why: After swallowed eggs hatch, Ascaris larvae pass through the liver and lungs, causing eosinophilic pneumonitis (Löffler syndrome), and are then swallowed to mature in the intestine. **Eggs appear in stool only after the prepatent period of about 2–3 months**, so stool is negative during the lung phase; larvae are occasionally seen in sputum.

whyNot.0: No method, including concentration, can find eggs that are not yet being produced.
whyNot.1: Adult female Ascaris produce very large numbers of eggs every day once mature.
whyNot.3: Ascaris is acquired by swallowing embryonated eggs, not by skin penetration.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, intestinal nematodes (Ascaris); CDC DPDx, Ascariasis

items.stem: A lymphatic filariasis survey in a Philippine province must test residents at a daytime community clinic. Which test can reliably detect Wuchereria bancrofti infection in blood collected at any hour?
options: Giemsa-stained thick film of daytime blood
Knott concentration of daytime venous blood
Rapid test for circulating filarial antigen
items.why: W. bancrofti microfilariae in the Philippines are nocturnally periodic, so they are scarce in daytime blood and films must be collected at night (about 10 p.m. to 2 a.m.). **Rapid immunochromatographic tests for circulating filarial antigen**, which is released by the adult worms, work on blood taken at any time and are used in mapping and transmission assessment surveys; they detect W. bancrofti but not Brugia.

whyNot.0: Because of nocturnal periodicity, microfilariae are few or absent in daytime blood, so a day film often misses the infection.
whyNot.1: Concentration improves sensitivity but cannot find microfilariae that are not circulating during the day.
whyNot.3: Skin snips are used for Onchocerca volvulus, whose microfilariae live in the skin, not for W. bancrofti.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Lymphatic filariasis; WHO Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis, monitoring and epidemiological assessment manual; Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, filarial worms

items.stem: A patient receiving high-dose corticosteroids for an autoimmune disease develops gram-negative bacteremia, abdominal pain and respiratory distress. Sputum shows slender larvae with a notched tail. Which feature of the parasite's life cycle best explains this severe illness?
options: Ingestion of embryonated eggs from moist soil
Autoinfection, as larvae become infective within the host
Inoculation of larvae through a mosquito bite
Encystment of larvae in muscle after eating raw pork
items.why: Strongyloides stercoralis rhabditiform larvae can develop into filariform larvae inside the bowel and reinvade the bowel wall or perianal skin. **This autoinfection lets the worm persist for decades and, with corticosteroids or HTLV-1 infection, multiply into hyperinfection or disseminated disease**, with larvae in sputum and enteric bacteria carried into the blood.

whyNot.0: Ingesting embryonated eggs is how Ascaris and Trichuris are acquired; it does not explain a massive larval burden.
whyNot.2: Mosquitoes transmit filarial worms, not Strongyloides.
whyNot.3: Larvae encysting in muscle after eating raw pork describes Trichinella.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, intestinal nematodes (Strongyloides); CDC DPDx, Strongyloidiasis

items.stem: A 3-year-old who often eats soil and plays with puppies has an enlarged liver, wheezing and marked eosinophilia. Visceral larva migrans from Toxocara canis is suspected. Which test best supports the diagnosis?
options: Thick blood film for migrating larvae
Serum ELISA with Toxocara larval antigens
items.why: Humans are accidental hosts in whom Toxocara larvae wander through tissues but never mature into adult worms. **Because no eggs are produced, diagnosis relies on serology (ELISA with excretory-secretory antigens)** together with eosinophilia and clinical findings, or rarely larvae in tissue.

whyNot.0: No adult worms develop in the human intestine, so no eggs appear in stool.
whyNot.1: The cellulose-tape preparation is used for Enterobius vermicularis eggs.
whyNot.2: Toxocara larvae migrate through tissues and are not seen in blood films.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, tissue nematodes and larva migrans; CDC DPDx, Toxocariasis

items.stem: An overseas worker returning from Egypt has blood in the urine, and Schistosoma haematobium is suspected. How should urine be collected to give the best chance of finding eggs?
options: Terminal portion of urine collected near midday
Midstream urine collected after an overnight fast
items.why: S. haematobium adults live in the veins around the bladder, and eggs with a terminal spine are passed in urine. **Egg output peaks around midday, and the last portion of the stream carries the most eggs**, so a terminal midday specimen, concentrated by sedimentation or filtration, is preferred.

whyNot.0: First-morning urine is not collected at the time of peak egg output.
whyNot.1: Bedtime urine is not collected at the time of peak egg output.
whyNot.3: Fasting does not affect egg output, and a midstream sample misses the egg-rich last portion.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Schistosomiasis; Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, blood flukes; Mahon & Lehman 7e, parasitology chapter

items.stem: A shepherd's son has a slowly enlarging liver cyst. Fluid aspirated before the cyst was recognized contains many small protoscolices with hooklets ('hydatid sand'). How did the patient most likely acquire this infection?
options: Eating undercooked lamb containing hydatid cysts
