Swallowing eggs passed in the feces of infected dogs
Larvae penetrating the skin while walking barefoot
Eating raw freshwater fish containing plerocercoids
items.why: Echinococcus granulosus adults live in the intestine of dogs, which pass eggs in their feces. **Humans become accidental intermediate hosts by swallowing these eggs**, which hatch and form hydatid cysts in the liver or lungs; eating infected organs is how dogs, not humans, become infected.

whyNot.0: Eating hydatid cysts in offal infects dogs, the definitive host; it does not cause hydatid disease in humans.
whyNot.2: Skin penetration by larvae is the route for hookworms and Strongyloides.
whyNot.3: Plerocercoids in raw fish transmit Diphyllobothrium.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, cestodes (Echinococcus); CDC DPDx, Echinococcosis

items.stem: A patient with megaloblastic anemia often ate raw freshwater fish while working near lakes in northern Europe. A stool concentrate shows oval, yellow-brown eggs about 65 × 45 µm with an inconspicuous operculum and a small knob at the opposite end. Which parasite is most likely?
items.why: D. latum, the broad fish tapeworm, is acquired by eating plerocercoid larvae in raw fish and can take up enough vitamin B12 to cause megaloblastic anemia. **It is the human tapeworm that passes operculated, unembryonated eggs**, usually with a small knob at the abopercular end.

whyNot.1: Clonorchis eggs are much smaller (about 27–35 µm) with a shouldered operculum.
whyNot.2: Fasciola eggs are much larger (about 130–150 µm) and are acquired from water plants.
whyNot.3: Taenia eggs are round with a radially striated shell and a hooked oncosphere, and have no operculum.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, cestodes; CDC DPDx, Diphyllobothriasis

items.stem: A routine stool examination of an asymptomatic food handler shows, in an iodine-stained concentrate, spherical cysts measuring 13–15 µm with a calibrated ocular micrometer. Mature cysts have four nuclei with small central karyosomes and even peripheral chromatin, and a trichrome smear shows chromatoid bodies with blunt, rounded ends. No trophozoites are seen. How should this be reported?
items.why: Cysts larger than 10 µm with up to four Entamoeba-type nuclei and blunt-ended chromatoid bodies fit the E. histolytica group, but **E. histolytica cysts cannot be told apart from those of nonpathogenic E. dispar by microscopy**, so they are reported as E. histolytica/E. dispar unless an E. histolytica-specific antigen test or PCR, or trophozoites containing red cells, settles it.

whyNot.0: E. coli cysts are usually larger, have up to eight nuclei with eccentric karyosomes and uneven peripheral chromatin, and have splinter-ended chromatoid bodies.
whyNot.1: E. hartmanni cysts look similar but measure less than 10 µm, which is why cysts must be measured with a calibrated micrometer.
whyNot.3: Microscopy cannot confirm E. histolytica, because nonpathogenic E. dispar looks identical; a specific antigen test or PCR is needed before reporting E. histolytica alone.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, intestinal amoebae; CDC DPDx, Amebiasis

items.stem: A soft contact lens wearer who rinses her lenses in homemade saline has severe eye pain and a ring-shaped corneal infiltrate. Bacterial and fungal cultures are negative. Which culture method is most appropriate for the corneal scraping?
options: Sheep blood agar incubated in 5% CO2
Non-nutrient agar with an E. coli overlay
items.why: Acanthamoeba keratitis is linked to contact lens wear and contaminated lens solutions or water. **Free-living amoebae are cultured on non-nutrient agar seeded with E. coli (or Enterobacter)**, which they feed on, leaving tracks; wrinkled double-walled cysts and trophozoites with spiky acanthopodia can then be seen.

whyNot.0: Sabouraud dextrose agar is a fungal medium.
whyNot.1: Sheep blood agar is for bacteria and does not provide the bacterial lawn the amoebae feed on.
whyNot.2: Diamond's TYM medium is used to culture Trichomonas vaginalis.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Free-living amebic infections; Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, free-living amoebae

items.stem: A trichrome-stained stool smear shows many round bodies that vary widely in size, from about 6 to 30 µm. Each has a large central area that fills most of the cell, with a thin rim of cytoplasm containing two to four small nuclei pressed against the edge. A trainee calls them yeasts. What should be reported?
items.why: This is the central body (vacuolar) form of Blastocystis, the form most often seen in stool. **A large central body that pushes a thin band of cytoplasm and nuclei to the edge, with wide size variation**, is characteristic; its role in disease is still debated, and it is usually reported with a semi-quantitative estimate.

whyNot.1: Yeasts are smaller (about 3–8 µm), oval, and show budding or pseudohyphae; they have no central body with peripheral nuclei.
whyNot.2: Iodamoeba cysts have a single nucleus with a large karyosome beside a big glycogen vacuole, and their shape is often irregular.
whyNot.3: Giardia cysts are oval, 8–12 µm, with four nuclei, axonemes and median bodies.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Blastocystis; Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, intestinal protozoa

items.stem: A hog raiser has dysentery. A saline wet mount of fresh stool shows a large oval organism about 70 µm long, covered with cilia and moving in a rotary fashion, with a big kidney-shaped nucleus. Which parasite is it?
items.why: Balantidium coli (now often called Neobalantidium coli) is the only ciliate that infects humans, and pigs are its main reservoir. **Its trophozoite is the largest intestinal protozoan, with cilia and a kidney-shaped macronucleus**, and it can cause ulcerative dysentery similar to amebiasis.

whyNot.0: E. histolytica moves by pseudopods, has no cilia, and has a single round nucleus.
whyNot.2: Giardia is a much smaller flagellate with two nuclei and a sucking disk.
whyNot.3: Chilomastix is a small, nonpathogenic flagellate with a spiral groove.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, intestinal ciliates; CDC DPDx, Balantidiasis

items.stem: A stool collection kit for ova and parasite examination contains two preservative vials. One is 10% formalin, used for the concentration procedure. Which preservative is usually in the second vial, used for the permanent trichrome-stained smear?
items.why: Formalin preserves eggs, larvae and cysts well for concentration but is less suited to trichrome staining of protozoa. **PVA fixative contains an adhesive that helps stool stick to the slide and preserves protozoan morphology for permanent stains**; mercury-free (zinc- or copper-based) versions are now widely used.

whyNot.0: Cary-Blair medium is for transporting stool for bacterial culture.
whyNot.1: Buffered glycerol saline is a transport medium for enteric bacteria such as Shigella.
whyNot.3: Saline does not preserve parasites, which deteriorate quickly in it.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, parasitology chapter (specimen collection and preservation); CDC DPDx, stool specimen collection and preservation

items.stem: A fresh liquid stool is received within 30 minutes of passage. The technologist prepares only an iodine wet mount to look for motile amebic trophozoites. Why is this approach inadequate?
options: Iodine kills trophozoites, so motility cannot be seen
Iodine dissolves the cyst wall of Entamoeba
Iodine stains helminth eggs too darkly to see
Iodine is meant for use on formed stools only
items.why: Iodine stains glycogen and nuclei, which helps in identifying cysts, but it kills trophozoites. **Motility must be looked for in a saline wet mount**, so fresh liquid stools should get both a saline and an iodine mount.

whyNot.1: Iodine does not dissolve cysts; it makes their nuclei and glycogen easier to see.
whyNot.2: Helminth eggs remain easy to recognize in an iodine mount.
whyNot.3: Iodine mounts can be prepared from any stool or concentrate.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, parasitology chapter (direct wet mounts); CDC DPDx, diagnostic procedures for stool specimens

items.stem: Which practice is correct when examining a stool concentrate wet mount under a 22 × 22 mm coverslip?
options: Scan central fields at 40× and stop at the first parasite found
Scan the whole coverslip at 10×, using 40× on suspect objects
Scan the whole coverslip under oil immersion at 100×
Scan only the coverslip edges at 10×, where eggs collect
items.why: Parasites may be few and mixed infections are common, so the whole coverslip must be examined systematically. **The entire coverslip is scanned at low power (10×) in overlapping rows, with high dry (40×) used for suspicious objects and small protozoa**, and finding one organism does not end the examination.

whyNot.0: Looking at only part of the coverslip and stopping at the first finding misses scant or mixed infections.
whyNot.2: Oil immersion is not used to scan wet mounts; it is impractical and too slow for the whole coverslip.
whyNot.3: Organisms are spread throughout the preparation, so scanning only the edges misses them.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman 7e, parasitology chapter (ova and parasite examination); CDC DPDx, diagnostic procedures

items.stem: Blood cultures for an adult with suspected sepsis are collected with a winged (butterfly) set and a tube holder directly into one aerobic and one anaerobic bottle. Which collection practice is recommended?
options: Fill both bottles well above the fill line to raise the yield
Refrigerate both bottles until they are sent to the laboratory
Fill the aerobic bottle first, then the anaerobic bottle
Fill the anaerobic bottle first, then the aerobic bottle
items.why: The tubing of a winged set contains air, and that air is drawn into whichever bottle is filled first. **With a winged set, the aerobic bottle is filled first so that air from the tubing does not enter the anaerobic bottle.** When a needle and syringe are used instead, the anaerobic bottle is usually inoculated first.

whyNot.0: Overfilling changes the blood-to-broth ratio the system is designed for and can cause false-positive instrument signals; bottles are filled to the marked volume.
whyNot.1: Blood culture bottles are kept at room temperature until loaded; refrigeration can kill fastidious organisms and delay detection.
whyNot.3: Filling the anaerobic bottle first would carry the air trapped in the tubing into it, adding oxygen that can hinder strict anaerobes.

items.ref: CLSI M47, Principles and Procedures for Blood Cultures; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., bloodstream infections chapter

items.stem: A stool specimen for Salmonella and Shigella culture is collected at a rural health unit and will reach the hospital laboratory about 6 hours later. How should it be sent?
options: Unpreserved in a sterile cup at room temperature
items.why: Unpreserved stool should be plated within about 1–2 hours, because the pH falls as normal flora multiply and acid-sensitive pathogens such as Shigella die off. **Cary-Blair is a buffered, low-nutrient transport medium that keeps enteric pathogens alive without letting them multiply.** It is the usual choice when stool cannot be plated promptly.

whyNot.0: Selenite F is an enrichment broth that is inoculated in the laboratory and subcultured after a short incubation; it is not a transport medium.
whyNot.1: Left unpreserved for 6 hours, the stool becomes acidic and overgrown by normal flora, so Shigella in particular may not be recovered.
whyNot.3: Formalin kills bacteria; it preserves parasites for microscopy and makes the stool useless for culture.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., specimen management chapter; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., gastrointestinal infections chapter

items.stem: A child bitten by a rat 10 days ago has fever, a rash on the hands and feet, and painful joints. Rat-bite fever caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis is suspected. What should the laboratory keep in mind when culturing the blood?
options: Only serum, not whole blood, can be cultured for it
SPS in standard blood culture bottles can inhibit it
It grows only at 42 °C in a microaerobic atmosphere
Blood must be refrigerated until it is inoculated
items.why: SPS is added to most blood culture broths as an anticoagulant that also blocks complement, phagocytosis and aminoglycosides, but it inhibits a few organisms. **Streptobacillus moniliformis is inhibited by SPS**, so blood is cultured in SPS-free broth, often enriched with serum, and the laboratory should be told of the suspicion. Some Neisseria species, Gardnerella vaginalis and Peptostreptococcus anaerobius are also SPS-sensitive.

whyNot.0: Whole blood, and joint fluid if present, is cultured; separating serum is not part of bacterial blood culture and would leave organisms trapped in the clot.
whyNot.2: These conditions are used for Campylobacter jejuni; S. moniliformis grows at 35–37 °C in an enriched medium, often with added CO2.
whyNot.3: Blood culture specimens are never refrigerated, since cold can kill fastidious organisms.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., chapter on Streptobacillus moniliformis and blood culture media; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed.

items.stem: A wound swab grows Proteus mirabilis that swarms over the entire sheep blood agar plate, hiding any other colonies. Which medium, added to the plating set, would best allow Staphylococcus aureus in the same specimen to be picked as separate colonies?
items.why: Phenylethyl alcohol inhibits facultative gram-negative bacilli by disrupting their membranes, while gram-positive organisms still grow. **On PEA agar, Proteus cannot swarm, so gram-positive cocci appear as isolated colonies.** Colistin–nalidixic acid (CNA) blood agar serves the same purpose.

whyNot.0: Eosin methylene blue agar selects for gram-negative bacteria and inhibits gram-positive cocci.
whyNot.1: Chocolate agar is enriched but not selective, so Proteus would still spread across it.
whyNot.2: MacConkey agar contains bile salts and crystal violet that inhibit gram-positive bacteria, so S. aureus would not grow.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., culture media chapter; Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., culture media chapter

items.stem: Haemophilus influenzae grows well on chocolate agar but usually fails to grow on sheep blood agar, even though sheep blood contains heme. What best explains this?
options: Sheep blood agar is too acidic to support Haemophilus
Sheep red cells lack hemin (X factor) entirely
Sheep blood NADases break down V factor (NAD)
Sheep blood agar has antibiotics that inhibit Haemophilus
items.why: H. influenzae needs both X factor (hemin) and V factor (NAD). On sheep blood agar the red cells are intact, and **sheep blood contains NADase enzymes that destroy V factor**, so too little NAD is available. Heating the blood to make chocolate agar lyses the cells, releasing both factors and inactivating the NADases.

whyNot.0: Sheep blood agar is buffered near neutral pH, which suits Haemophilus; pH is not the problem.
whyNot.1: Sheep red cells do contain heme; the limiting nutrient on this medium is V factor, not X factor.
whyNot.3: Plain sheep blood agar is a nonselective medium with no added antibiotics.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Haemophilus chapter; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Haemophilus chapter

items.stem: A blood culture isolate from a patient with native-valve endocarditis is a catalase-positive, gram-positive coccus in clusters. The slide (clumping factor) test is positive, but the tube coagulase test is negative at 4 and 24 hours. It is PYR positive and ornithine decarboxylase positive. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: S. lugdunensis has a clumping factor, so it can give a positive slide or latex test, but it lacks free coagulase and is tube coagulase negative. **A positive PYR test and positive ornithine decarboxylase separate S. lugdunensis from S. aureus.** It behaves more like S. aureus than other coagulase-negative staphylococci and causes aggressive native-valve endocarditis.

whyNot.0: S. saprophyticus is a urinary pathogen that is clumping factor negative and resistant to novobiocin.
whyNot.1: S. epidermidis is negative in the slide clumping test and is usually PYR negative.
whyNot.3: S. aureus is tube coagulase positive and PYR negative.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Staphylococcus chapter; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., staphylococci chapter

items.stem: Blood culture bottles from a patient with endocarditis flag positive, and the Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Subculture to sheep blood agar shows no growth after 48 hours, but tiny colonies appear on a second sheep blood agar plate next to a cross-streak of Staphylococcus aureus. What do these organisms require?
items.why: These are nutritionally variant streptococci (Abiotrophia and Granulicatella), which grow in blood culture broth but not on unsupplemented agar. **They need pyridoxal, which S. aureus releases, so they grow as satellite colonies around the staphylococcal streak.** Media supplemented with pyridoxal (or L-cysteine) support their growth, and a pyridoxal disk confirms the requirement.

whyNot.0: Vitamin B12 is not the growth factor that S. aureus supplies to these streptococci, and it is not their characteristic requirement.
whyNot.2: V factor explains why Haemophilus satellites around S. aureus, but the Gram stain rules Haemophilus out here.
whyNot.3: X factor is a Haemophilus requirement; Haemophilus is a gram-negative coccobacillus, not a gram-positive coccus in chains.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Streptococcus, Enterococcus and similar organisms chapter; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., streptococci chapter

items.stem: When a throat swab is plated on sheep blood agar to look for group A streptococci, the technologist stabs the loop several times into the agar. What is the purpose of these stabs?
options: To produce a CAMP reaction around the colonies
To check the motility of the isolate within the agar
To expose streptolysin S to more oxygen so it is activated
To reveal hemolysis by oxygen-labile streptolysin O
items.why: Group A streptococci make two hemolysins. Streptolysin S is oxygen-stable and acts at the surface, but **streptolysin O is inactivated by oxygen, so its hemolysis is seen best in the reduced conditions below the surface**. Stabbing, or anaerobic incubation, helps reveal beta-hemolysis by strains that make mainly streptolysin O.

whyNot.0: The CAMP test needs a cross-streak of a beta-lysin-producing S. aureus and is used for group B streptococci.
whyNot.1: Motility is tested in semisolid media, and streptococci are nonmotile.
whyNot.2: Streptolysin S is already oxygen-stable; the stabs create low-oxygen conditions rather than adding oxygen.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., streptococci chapter; Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed.

items.stem: A nasopharyngeal swab from a healthy child in a carriage study grows oxidase-positive, gram-negative diplococci on modified Thayer-Martin agar. The isolate produces acid from glucose, maltose and lactose, and the ONPG test is positive. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Neisseria species are separated by the sugars they use. **Acid from lactose with a positive ONPG (beta-galactosidase) test identifies N. lactamica**, a harmless nasopharyngeal commensal that can grow on selective gonococcal media. N. meningitidis uses glucose and maltose but not lactose.

whyNot.0: N. meningitidis uses glucose and maltose but is lactose and ONPG negative.
whyNot.1: M. catarrhalis produces no acid from these sugars and is identified by butyrate esterase and DNase.
whyNot.3: N. gonorrhoeae produces acid from glucose only.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Neisseria and Moraxella chapter

items.stem: A patient has had sustained fever for 6 days. A blood culture grows a non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. TSI shows an alkaline slant and acid butt with no gas and only a small amount of blackening near the stab line. It is motile, lysine decarboxylase positive, ornithine decarboxylase negative, and citrate negative. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Typhoid fever is a bacteremic illness, and blood culture gives the best yield in the first week. **S. Typhi typically gives K/A with no gas and only a small wisp of H2S, and it is citrate and ornithine negative**, unlike most other salmonellae. Its positive lysine decarboxylase also separates it from Citrobacter.

whyNot.0: Citrobacter freundii is lysine decarboxylase negative and usually citrate positive.
whyNot.1: Non-typhoidal serovars such as Enteritidis usually produce gas and abundant H2S and are ornithine and citrate positive.
whyNot.2: Shigella is nonmotile and does not produce H2S.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Enterobacterales chapter; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Enterobacteriaceae chapter

items.stem: Two H2S-positive, non-lactose-fermenting stool isolates both give K/A with H2S on TSI. On lysine iron agar (LIA), isolate 1 shows a purple slant and purple butt with blackening, whereas isolate 2 shows a purple slant and a yellow butt with blackening. Which organism best fits isolate 2?
items.why: In LIA, lysine decarboxylation makes the butt alkaline (purple), while a yellow butt means only glucose was fermented. **A yellow butt with H2S points to a lysine-negative, H2S-positive organism such as Citrobacter**, whereas Salmonella is lysine positive, as isolate 1 is. Proteus and related genera deaminate lysine and give a red slant.

whyNot.1: Most Salmonella decarboxylate lysine and give a purple butt, as isolate 1 did.
whyNot.2: Edwardsiella tarda is lysine decarboxylase positive and would give a purple butt.
whyNot.3: Proteus deaminates lysine, producing a red (burgundy) slant rather than a purple one.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Enterobacteriaceae chapter; MacFaddin, Biochemical Tests for Identification of Medical Bacteria, 3rd ed.

items.stem: Several people develop watery diarrhea and cramps the day after eating raw oysters. Stool on TCBS agar yields green colonies of an oxidase-positive, curved gram-negative rod that grows in broth with 6% NaCl but not in broth without added salt. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Most pathogenic vibrios are halophilic and need added salt, the main exception being V. cholerae. **V. parahaemolyticus does not ferment sucrose, so it forms green colonies on TCBS**, and it is a common cause of diarrhea after eating raw or undercooked seafood.

whyNot.0: V. cholerae ferments sucrose, forming yellow colonies on TCBS, and grows in broth without added salt.
whyNot.2: V. alginolyticus ferments sucrose and forms yellow colonies on TCBS.
whyNot.3: Aeromonas does not need salt and grows poorly on TCBS; it is usually recovered on blood agar or CIN agar.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Vibrio, Aeromonas, Plesiomonas and Chromobacterium chapter

items.stem: A stool isolate from a patient with diarrhea after eating raw shellfish is a non-lactose fermenter on MacConkey agar. It gives K/A without H2S on TSI and agglutinates in Shigella group D (S. sonnei) antiserum. Before Shigella is reported, which simple test should be done?
items.why: Plesiomonas shigelloides shares a somatic antigen with S. sonnei and can be mistaken for it in slide agglutination. **Plesiomonas is oxidase positive, whereas Shigella is oxidase negative**, so an oxidase test on growth from a nonselective medium such as blood agar prevents a false Shigella report.

whyNot.0: Neither organism produces H2S.
whyNot.1: Both organisms are usually catalase positive, so catalase does not separate them.
whyNot.3: Both ferment glucose, so the O-F test reads fermentative for each.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Vibrio, Aeromonas, Plesiomonas and Chromobacterium chapter

items.stem: A gastric antral biopsy from a patient with a duodenal ulcer is placed in a gel containing urea and phenol red. Within an hour the gel turns from yellow to pink-red. What causes this color change?
options: Urease from Helicobacter pylori releasing ammonia from urea
Catalase from Helicobacter pylori releasing oxygen
Acid from Helicobacter pylori fermenting glucose in the gel
Gastric acid carried into the gel with the biopsy
items.why: H. pylori produces large amounts of urease, which splits urea into ammonia and CO2. **The ammonia raises the pH, turning phenol red from yellow to pink-red**, so a positive rapid urease test on a biopsy is presumptive evidence of H. pylori. The urea breath test relies on the same enzyme.

whyNot.1: Catalase releases oxygen bubbles from hydrogen peroxide and does not change a pH indicator.
whyNot.2: H. pylori does not ferment carbohydrates, and acid would keep phenol red yellow rather than turn it pink.
whyNot.3: Gastric acid would lower the pH and keep the gel yellow.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Campylobacter, Arcobacter and Helicobacter chapter

items.stem: Two blood culture sets are drawn by separate venipunctures from a febrile patient with no intravascular catheter or prosthetic device. After 3 days, only the aerobic bottle of one set grows a coagulase-negative staphylococcus; the other set remains negative. How is this finding best interpreted?
options: Endocarditis, since staphylococci grew from blood
True bacteremia, since any growth from blood is significant
Infection of an indwelling central venous catheter
Probable contamination from skin flora during collection
items.why: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are the most common blood culture contaminants. **A skin organism growing late in only one of two independently drawn sets, in a patient without devices, most likely reflects contamination.** True bacteremia is suggested when the same organism grows in several separately collected sets.

whyNot.0: Endocarditis causes continuous bacteremia, so most or all sets would be expected to be positive.
whyNot.1: Skin commensals in only one of several sets are usually contaminants; treating every isolate as significant leads to unnecessary antibiotics.
whyNot.2: The patient has no intravascular catheter, so a line infection is unlikely.

items.ref: CLSI M47, Principles and Procedures for Blood Cultures; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., bloodstream infections chapter

items.stem: Within a day of a cat bite, a woman's hand becomes red, swollen and very painful. A Gram stain of pus from the wound shows small gram-negative coccobacilli. Which set of findings on the isolate best supports Pasteurella multocida?
options: Oxidase negative, indole positive, pink colonies on MacConkey agar
Oxidase positive, indole positive, no growth on MacConkey agar
Oxidase positive, catalase negative, colonies that pit the agar
Growth only beside an S. aureus streak on sheep blood agar
items.why: P. multocida is part of the oral flora of cats and dogs and causes rapidly progressing cellulitis after bites or scratches. **Oxidase and indole positivity together with no growth on MacConkey agar point to P. multocida** among small gram-negative coccobacilli from animal bites. Unlike most gram-negative rods, it is usually susceptible to penicillin.

whyNot.0: Oxidase-negative rods that grow and ferment lactose on MacConkey agar fit Escherichia coli and other Enterobacterales, not Pasteurella.
whyNot.2: A catalase-negative, oxidase-positive organism that pits the agar suggests Eikenella corrodens, which is linked to human bites.
whyNot.3: Satellite growth beside S. aureus reflects the V-factor need of Haemophilus; P. multocida grows well on sheep blood agar alone.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Pasteurella and similar organisms chapter

items.stem: A urinary catheter specimen from an ICU patient grows an oxidase-negative gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose on MacConkey agar overnight. Colonies left at room temperature turn red. The isolate is DNase positive and gelatinase positive. What is the most likely identification?
items.why: Serratia marcescens is an opportunistic hospital pathogen often linked to catheters and contaminated solutions. **Red prodigiosin pigment, best produced at room temperature, together with positive DNase and gelatinase, points to S. marcescens.** Not every strain is pigmented, so the biochemical results remain important.

whyNot.0: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is oxidase positive and makes blue-green, not red, pigment.
whyNot.2: Escherichia coli usually ferments lactose rapidly and is DNase negative.
whyNot.3: Klebsiella pneumoniae ferments lactose, forms mucoid pink colonies on MacConkey agar, and is DNase negative.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Enterobacterales chapter

items.stem: A kidney transplant recipient has a lung nodule and a brain abscess. A sputum Gram stain shows thin, beaded, branching gram-positive rods. With a modified Kinyoun stain using 1% sulfuric acid as decolorizer the filaments are partly red, but they are not acid-fast by the standard Ziehl-Neelsen method. Dry, chalky white colonies with an earthy odor grow aerobically after several days. What is the most likely organism?
items.why: Nocardia are aerobic, branching, beaded gram-positive rods that cause lung and brain infections in immunocompromised hosts. **Their cell walls are only partially acid-fast, so they keep carbol fuchsin when a weak acid such as 1% sulfuric acid is the decolorizer, but not with acid-alcohol.** Chalky, dry colonies with an earthy odor are typical.

whyNot.1: Streptomyces also forms chalky, earthy colonies but is not acid-fast, even with the modified method.
whyNot.2: Actinomyces israelii is an anaerobe and is not acid-fast by any method.
whyNot.3: M. tuberculosis is strongly acid-fast with acid-alcohol and does not form branching filaments.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Nocardia, Streptomyces, Rhodococcus and similar organisms chapter

items.stem: A lactose-fermenting Escherichia coli control strain is inoculated into TSI agar. The tube is forgotten and read after 48 hours, showing a red (alkaline) slant over a yellow (acid) butt. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The cap was too tight, so acid could not form on the slant
The butt was not stabbed, so the organism grew only on the slant
After the sugars ran out, peptone breakdown on the slant raised the pH
The strain has lost the ability to ferment lactose and sucrose
items.why: TSI is read at 18–24 hours. **Read too late, a lactose or sucrose fermenter can show a false K/A, because once the carbohydrates are used up the organisms on the aerobic slant break down peptones and release alkaline products.** The control should be repeated and read at the correct time.

whyNot.0: A tight cap limits oxygen and tends to favor acid reactions; it does not create an alkaline slant. TSI is incubated with a loose cap.
whyNot.1: Without a stab the butt would show little or no reaction, not a yellow acid butt.
whyNot.3: A change in a stable control strain is far less likely than a timing error; read at 18–24 hours it still ferments lactose and sucrose.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., Enterobacteriaceae chapter; MacFaddin, Biochemical Tests for Identification of Medical Bacteria, 3rd ed.

items.stem: Several clients develop draining skin abscesses at injection sites weeks after cosmetic injections at an unlicensed clinic. Pus grows an acid-fast bacillus that forms non-pigmented colonies within 5 days on subculture, grows on MacConkey agar without crystal violet, reduces nitrate, and is arylsulfatase positive at 3 days. Which organism is most likely?
items.why: Rapidly growing mycobacteria form mature colonies in under 7 days and commonly cause skin and soft tissue infections after injections, surgery or exposure to contaminated water. **Growth in under 7 days, growth on MacConkey agar, a positive 3-day arylsulfatase and positive nitrate reduction fit M. fortuitum**, whereas M. chelonae and M. abscessus are nitrate negative.

whyNot.0: M. marinum is a slow-growing photochromogen that grows best near 30 °C and is linked to fish tanks and water.
whyNot.1: M. tuberculosis is a slow grower that needs several weeks to form colonies and does not grow on MacConkey agar.
whyNot.3: M. avium complex is slow growing and nitrate negative.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Mycobacteria chapter; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., mycobacteria chapter

items.stem: A busy TB laboratory changes its screening stain for sputum smears from Ziehl-Neelsen to auramine-rhodamine. What is the main advantage of the fluorochrome stain?
options: It separates M. tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria
It no longer needs a decolorizing step
Positive smears never need checking by another method
Smears can be screened faster at lower magnification
items.why: Acid-fast bacilli stained with auramine-rhodamine glow yellow-green against a dark background. **Because they stand out so clearly, smears can be screened at lower magnification, covering more area in less time and with greater sensitivity than carbol fuchsin stains.** Positive or doubtful smears can be confirmed with a Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun stain.

whyNot.0: All mycobacteria stain alike; species identification needs culture or molecular tests.
whyNot.1: Fluorochrome staining still uses an acid-alcohol decolorizer, followed by a quenching counterstain such as potassium permanganate.
whyNot.2: Laboratories often confirm positive or doubtful fluorochrome smears, for example by restaining with a carbol fuchsin method.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., mycobacteria chapter; Global Laboratory Initiative (WHO/Stop TB), Laboratory Diagnosis of Tuberculosis by Sputum Microscopy: The Handbook (2013)

items.stem: Endocervical cells are centrifuged onto cycloheximide-treated McCoy cell monolayers. After 48–72 hours the monolayer is stained with iodine and shows brown-staining intracytoplasmic inclusions. Which organism do these inclusions indicate?
items.why: Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular bacteria, so culture needs living cells, and McCoy cells are a standard line for C. trachomatis. **C. trachomatis inclusions contain glycogen and stain brown with iodine**, whereas those of C. psittaci and C. pneumoniae do not. Nucleic acid amplification tests have now largely replaced culture for routine diagnosis.

whyNot.0: Herpes simplex virus causes cell rounding and syncytia with intranuclear inclusions, not iodine-staining cytoplasmic inclusions.
whyNot.1: C. psittaci inclusions lack glycogen and do not stain with iodine.
whyNot.2: Mycoplasma genitalium is a cell wall-deficient bacterium that does not form glycogen inclusions and is detected by NAAT.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., Chlamydia chapter; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., obligate intracellular bacteria chapter

items.stem: A 100-mL sample of treated drinking water is passed through a 0.45-µm membrane filter. The filter is placed on m-Endo medium and incubated at 35 °C for 24 hours. Which colonies are counted as coliforms?
options: Red colonies with a golden-green metallic sheen
Yellow colonies surrounded by a yellow zone
items.why: In the membrane filter method, bacteria in a measured volume of water are trapped on a filter that is then incubated on a selective, differential medium. **On m-Endo agar, coliforms ferment lactose and form red colonies with a golden-green metallic sheen**, which are counted per 100 mL. Fecal coliforms are counted separately on m-FC medium at 44.5 °C, where they form blue colonies.

whyNot.1: Blue colonies are the fecal (thermotolerant) coliform criterion on m-FC medium at 44.5 °C, not on m-Endo.
whyNot.2: Black-centered colonies indicate H2S production, as with Salmonella on media such as XLD, and are not the coliform criterion.
whyNot.3: A yellow zone around colonies is the mannitol salt agar reaction used for Staphylococcus aureus.

items.ref: APHA/AWWA/WEF, Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater, Method 9222 (membrane filter technique for coliforms)

items.stem: A patient has a thick, crumbly, yellowed toenail, and onychomycosis is suspected. How should the specimen for fungal culture be collected?
options: Soak the nail clippings in sterile saline in a sealed tube
Clip only the free outer edge, which is easiest to reach
Rub a saline-moistened cotton swab over the nail surface
Wipe with 70% alcohol, then scrape debris under the nail
items.why: Surface contaminants and bacteria are first reduced by wiping with 70% alcohol. **Fungi are most likely to be viable in the subungual debris and deeper diseased nail closest to the nail bed**, so that material is collected after the outer portion is discarded. The scrapings are sent dry in a clean container or paper packet.

whyNot.0: Moisture in a sealed tube lets bacteria and contaminating molds overgrow the slow-growing dermatophytes.
whyNot.1: The free outer edge holds mostly dead fungal elements plus contaminating molds and bacteria, so cultures are often negative or misleading.
whyNot.2: Swabs pick up surface contaminants and too little material and are unsuitable for dermatophyte culture.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., mycology chapter (specimen collection); Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., laboratory methods in basic mycology

items.stem: Four specimens for fungal culture arrive late in the evening and will be processed the next morning. Which one should be held at room temperature rather than refrigerated?
items.why: Most specimens for fungal culture that cannot be processed promptly are refrigerated at about 4 °C to limit overgrowth by bacteria. **CSF, like blood, is kept at room temperature, because it comes from a normally sterile site and some fungi lose viability in the cold.** Skin, hair and nail specimens are also held at room temperature.

whyNot.0: Sputum carries oral bacteria that overgrow fungi at room temperature, so it is refrigerated if processing is delayed.
whyNot.1: Bronchial washings contain oropharyngeal flora and are refrigerated when processing is delayed.
whyNot.2: Bacteria multiply in urine left at room temperature, so delayed urine is refrigerated.

items.ref: Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., laboratory methods in basic mycology; Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., mycology chapter

items.stem: A new influenza A subtype emerges after a human strain and an avian strain infect the same pig and exchange whole genes, and the new virus spreads worldwide. Which feature of influenza A makes this antigenic shift possible?
options: Its RNA polymerase introduces frequent point mutations
Its RNA genome is split into separate segments
Its DNA genome integrates into the host chromosome
Its lipid envelope is taken from the host cell membrane
items.why: Influenza A has eight separate RNA segments. **When two strains infect the same cell, whole segments such as the hemagglutinin gene can be swapped, producing a new subtype (antigenic shift).** Because few people have immunity to the new hemagglutinin or neuraminidase, shifts can cause pandemics.

whyNot.0: Point mutations from the error-prone polymerase cause antigenic drift, the gradual change behind seasonal epidemics.
whyNot.2: Influenza is an RNA virus that does not integrate into host DNA; integration is a feature of retroviruses.
whyNot.3: All enveloped viruses take membrane from the host, but this does not allow genes to be exchanged.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., influenza and respiratory viruses chapter; Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., virology chapter

items.stem: A 12-year-old had dengue caused by serotype 1 three years ago. She is now infected with serotype 2 and develops plasma leakage and shock. What best explains the higher risk of severe dengue in this second infection?
options: Reassortment between the two serotypes produced a more virulent subtype
Non-neutralizing antibodies from the first infection enhance virus entry into monocytes
No IgG persisted after the first infection, so she had no immunity at all
Virus from the first infection stayed latent in sensory ganglia and reactivated
items.why: Infection with one dengue serotype gives lasting immunity to that serotype but only brief cross-protection against the others. **In a later infection with a different serotype, cross-reactive but non-neutralizing antibodies can bind the virus and help it enter Fc receptor-bearing cells (antibody-dependent enhancement)**, raising the viral load and the risk of severe dengue.

whyNot.0: Dengue virus has a single, unsegmented RNA genome, so reassortment between serotypes does not occur.
whyNot.2: IgG from a past dengue infection persists for years; its cross-reactivity, not its absence, is linked to severe second infections.
whyNot.3: Latency in sensory ganglia is a feature of herpesviruses; dengue virus does not become latent.

items.ref: WHO, Dengue: Guidelines for Diagnosis, Treatment, Prevention and Control (2009); Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., arboviruses chapter

items.stem: Respiratory virus isolation is requested on a throat swab in viral transport medium, but the cell culture laboratory will not set it up until about 5 days later. Which storage condition best preserves the virus until then?
items.why: Specimens for viral culture can be refrigerated for short delays, usually up to 2–3 days. **For longer delays they should be frozen at −70 °C or below**, because storage at −20 °C allows ice crystals to form that damage virions and reduce infectivity. Repeated freezing and thawing should also be avoided.

whyNot.1: Ordinary −20 °C freezers allow ice crystal formation that destroys many viruses, so they are avoided.
whyNot.2: Refrigeration suits short delays only; infectivity declines over several days.
whyNot.3: Room temperature is the worst option, as many viruses, especially enveloped ones, lose infectivity quickly.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., virology chapter (specimen collection and transport); Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., virology chapter

items.stem: A man from a rural barangay who was bitten by a stray dog 6 weeks earlier is admitted with agitation, fear of water and excess salivation. Which antemortem specimen is most useful for detecting rabies virus antigen or RNA?
options: Nuchal skin biopsy that includes hair follicles
Stool collected in a clean, dry container
Urine sediment from a first-morning sample
EDTA whole blood collected during a fever spike
items.why: Rabies virus travels along nerves and does not produce a useful viremia. **Before death, the best specimens are a nuchal skin biopsy, where virus is found in nerves around hair follicles, together with saliva**, tested by immunofluorescence or RT-PCR; CSF and serum are used for antibody. Postmortem brain tissue tested by direct fluorescent antibody remains the reference method.

whyNot.1: The virus is not shed in stool.
whyNot.2: Urine is not a useful specimen for rabies diagnosis.
whyNot.3: Rabies virus is not reliably present in blood, so blood is not used to detect the virus.

items.ref: WHO, Laboratory Techniques in Rabies, 5th ed. (2018); CDC, Rabies diagnosis guidance

items.stem: Urine from a newborn with suspected congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is inoculated into shell vials containing MRC-5 fibroblasts on coverslips, centrifuged, and stained after 24–48 hours with a fluorescent monoclonal antibody. What does this method detect?
options: CMV early antigen in infected cell nuclei before CPE appears
Hemadsorption of guinea pig red cells onto the monolayer
CMV-specific IgM antibody in the infant's urine
Owl's-eye inclusions on a Giemsa stain of the urine sediment
items.why: Conventional tube cultures may need 1–3 weeks before CMV produces cytopathic effect. **In the shell vial method, centrifugation enhances infection and a monoclonal antibody detects early viral antigen in nuclei within 16–48 hours, well before CPE appears.** It gives a culture-based result much faster than tube culture.

whyNot.1: Hemadsorption detects viruses with surface hemagglutinin such as influenza and parainfluenza; CMV does not hemadsorb.
whyNot.2: The shell vial detects virus, not antibody, and IgM is not measured in urine.
whyNot.3: Owl's-eye inclusions are looked for directly in cells or tissue, not in cultured fibroblasts, and the method is insensitive.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., herpesviruses chapter; Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., virology chapter (cell culture and shell vial methods)

items.stem: Before an RNA virus such as dengue virus or SARS-CoV-2 can be detected by PCR, its RNA must first be copied into DNA. Which enzyme performs this step?
items.why: PCR uses a DNA polymerase that copies DNA templates. **For RNA targets such as dengue virus or SARS-CoV-2, reverse transcriptase first makes complementary DNA (cDNA) from the RNA**, which is then amplified; the combined method is called RT-PCR.

whyNot.0: Taq polymerase copies DNA during the extension step and needs a DNA template.
whyNot.1: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments and does not make DNA from RNA.
whyNot.2: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific sequences and are not used to convert RNA.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., molecular diagnostics chapter; Buckingham, Molecular Diagnostics: Fundamentals, Methods and Clinical Applications

items.stem: A molecular laboratory replaces dTTP with dUTP in all its PCR master mixes and adds uracil-N-glycosylase (UNG), which acts briefly before the first denaturation step. What problem is this designed to prevent?
options: Degradation of RNA templates by ribonucleases
Primer-dimer formation during the annealing step
False negatives caused by inhibitors such as heme
items.why: Because every amplicon the laboratory makes contains uracil, any that contaminate a new reaction can be destroyed. **UNG removes uracil from contaminating amplicons before cycling, so they cannot be amplified into a false-positive result**, while natural DNA templates, which contain thymine, are untouched. The enzyme is then inactivated by the heat of the first denaturation.

whyNot.0: RNase damage is prevented by RNase-free technique and RNase inhibitors; UNG acts on uracil-containing DNA.
whyNot.1: Primer-dimers are reduced by primer design and hot-start polymerases.
whyNot.2: Inhibitors are dealt with by better extraction, dilution and internal controls, not by UNG.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., molecular diagnostics chapter; Buckingham, Molecular Diagnostics: Fundamentals, Methods and Clinical Applications

items.stem: A real-time PCR for Salmonella on a stool specimen shows no amplification of the target, and the internal amplification control added to the same specimen also fails to amplify. The run's positive and negative controls are acceptable. How should the result be handled?
options: Reported as positive, since the target used up the control
Reported as invalid and repeated after re-extraction or dilution
Reported as a weak positive needing culture confirmation
items.why: An internal amplification control is added to each specimen to show that extraction and amplification worked in that tube. **If both the target and the internal control fail, the specimen probably contains inhibitors or was poorly extracted, so the result is invalid, not negative.** Re-extracting, diluting the extract or recollecting the specimen is appropriate; stool is a common source of inhibitors.

whyNot.0: A strong target can outcompete the internal control, but then the target itself would amplify.
whyNot.2: No target signal was seen, so there is no basis for calling the specimen positive.
whyNot.3: A negative result can be reported only when the internal control amplifies, proving the reaction could have detected the target.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., molecular diagnostics chapter; CLSI MM03, Molecular Diagnostic Methods for Infectious Diseases

items.stem: Continuous-monitoring blood culture instruments flag a bottle as positive without opening it. What do most of these systems detect?
options: Turbidity measured by light passing through the broth
Hemolysis of the red cells in the bottle
Rising CO2 from microbial growth, read by a bottle sensor
items.why: Growing organisms release CO2 into the broth. **Systems such as BacT/ALERT and BACTEC read a colorimetric or fluorescent CO2 sensor at the bottom of each bottle every few minutes and flag the bottle when the signal rises.** Some other systems detect pressure changes from gas production or consumption.

whyNot.0: Blood makes the broth opaque, so turbidity is not a reliable automated signal; it is a sign used when bottles are inspected by eye.
whyNot.1: ATP bioluminescence is not the detection principle of routine blood culture instruments.
whyNot.2: Hemolysis may be seen by eye with some organisms but is not what these instruments measure.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., bloodstream infections chapter; Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., blood culture chapter

items.stem: Over three weeks, five infants in one neonatal ICU develop bloodstream infections with Klebsiella pneumoniae that share the same antibiogram. Infection control asks whether a single strain is spreading in the unit. Which laboratory approach best answers this?
options: Molecular typing of the isolates, such as whole-genome sequencing
Repeating the susceptibility tests by a second method
Identifying the isolates again with another biochemical kit
Comparing the colony counts in each positive blood culture
items.why: Matching species and antibiograms suggest, but do not prove, that isolates are related. **Molecular typing methods such as whole-genome sequencing or pulsed-field gel electrophoresis compare the strains' genomes and show whether the isolates are clonal**, which guides outbreak control.

whyNot.1: A second susceptibility method only confirms the antibiogram, which unrelated strains can share.
whyNot.2: Re-identification confirms the species but does not show whether the isolates are the same strain.
whyNot.3: Colony counts reflect the level of bacteremia, not how closely the strains are related.

items.ref: Mahon & Lehman, Textbook of Diagnostic Microbiology, 7th ed., infection prevention and control chapter; Tille, Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology, 15th ed., infection control chapter

items.stem: In a school-based deworming survey, a Kato-Katz thick smear made with a standard 41.7-mg template shows 210 Ascaris lumbricoides eggs. Using the usual multiplication factor and the WHO intensity classes for Ascaris (light 1–4,999 EPG; moderate 5,000–49,999 EPG; heavy ≥50,000 EPG), how is the result reported?
items.why: A 41.7-mg template holds about 1/24 of a gram, so the egg count is multiplied by 24 to give eggs per gram (EPG). **210 × 24 = 5,040 EPG, which falls in the moderate-intensity class for Ascaris.** Intensity classes guide mass drug administration and the measurement of its effect.

whyNot.0: This uses a factor of 10, as if the template held 100 mg of stool.
whyNot.1: This uses a factor of 20 instead of 24, which underestimates the count and puts it in the wrong class.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 240, a tenfold error that wrongly classes the infection as heavy.

items.ref: WHO, Helminth Control in School-Age Children, 2nd ed. (2011); WHO, Bench Aids for the Diagnosis of Intestinal Parasites, 2nd ed.

worked.problem: A 41.7-mg Kato-Katz smear shows 85 Trichuris trichiura eggs. Report the EPG and the WHO intensity class for Trichuris (light 1–999; moderate 1,000–9,999; heavy ≥10,000 EPG).
steps: Multiplication factor for a 41.7-mg template = 1,000 mg ÷ 41.7 mg ≈ 24

items.stem: A urine sediment from a 6-year-old girl shows colorless, thin-shelled eggs about 50–60 × 20–30 µm. They are flattened on one side, and several contain a coiled larva. What is the most likely identification?
options: Schistosoma haematobium eggs from the bladder wall
Trichuris trichiura eggs from fecal contamination
Enterobius vermicularis eggs from the perianal skin
items.why: Female pinworms lay their eggs on the perianal skin, and in young girls these can easily contaminate a voided urine specimen. **Colorless, thin-shelled eggs that are flattened on one side and contain a larva are Enterobius vermicularis eggs**; a cellulose-tape preparation confirms the infection.

whyNot.0: S. haematobium eggs are much larger, about 110–170 µm, and have a terminal spine.
whyNot.1: Trichuris eggs are barrel shaped and yellow-brown with a plug at each end.
whyNot.3: Hookworm eggs are oval and symmetrical and usually contain a cleaving embryo, not a larva.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Enterobiasis; Markell & Voge's Medical Parasitology, 10th ed., intestinal nematodes chapter

items.stem: After a beach holiday where dogs roam freely, a tourist develops an intensely itchy, raised, red, winding track on the sole of the foot that advances a few millimeters to a few centimeters each day. Repeated stool examinations are negative. Which parasite is most likely responsible?
options: Larvae of Ancylostoma braziliense, an animal hookworm
Larvae of the human hookworm Necator americanus
items.why: Humans are dead-end hosts for dog and cat hookworms, whose filariform larvae penetrate the skin but cannot complete their life cycle. **The larvae wander in the epidermis, producing the creeping, serpiginous track of cutaneous larva migrans**, and no eggs appear in the stool.

whyNot.0: Trichinella larvae are eaten in meat and encyst in skeletal muscle; they do not travel through the skin.
whyNot.2: Toxocara is acquired by swallowing eggs, and its larvae migrate through internal organs (visceral or ocular larva migrans), not the skin.
whyNot.3: N. americanus larvae cause ground itch but then migrate to the intestine, where the adults lay eggs that appear in stool.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Zoonotic hookworm (cutaneous larva migrans); Markell & Voge's Medical Parasitology, 10th ed.

items.stem: A stool specimen left at room temperature for more than a day before it is examined shows rhabditiform larvae with a long buccal canal and a small, inconspicuous genital primordium. No eggs are seen. What is the best interpretation?
options: Hookworm eggs hatched in the specimen after it was passed
Ascaris eggs hatched in the specimen after it was passed
Strongyloides stercoralis larvae passed in the stool
items.why: Hookworm eggs embryonate quickly, and in stool kept warm for a day or more they hatch into rhabditiform larvae. **A long buccal canal and an inconspicuous genital primordium identify these as hookworm larvae rather than Strongyloides larvae**, which have a short buccal canal and a prominent primordium. This is why stool for ova and parasite examination is examined fresh or preserved promptly.

whyNot.1: Filariform larvae are long and slender with a closed mouth, and those of Strongyloides have a notched tail; the larvae seen here are rhabditiform.
whyNot.2: Ascaris eggs need weeks in soil to embryonate and do not hatch in a stool specimen.
whyNot.3: Strongyloides rhabditiform larvae have a short buccal canal and a large genital primordium.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Hookworm and Strongyloidiasis; Markell & Voge's Medical Parasitology, 10th ed.

items.stem: Stool from a farmer in a lowland Philippine province contains straw-colored, operculated eggs about 85–115 × 55–70 µm. He often eats raw or lightly cooked freshwater snails (kuhol, Pila luzonica) as pulutan. Which fluke is most likely?
items.why: Echinostoma ilocanum (Garrison's fluke) is an intestinal fluke found in the Philippines. **Its metacercariae encyst in freshwater snails such as Pila luzonica, so eating these snails raw or undercooked transmits the infection.** The eggs are large, operculated and unembryonated when passed, resembling smaller versions of Fasciola-type eggs.

whyNot.1: Clonorchis sinensis is acquired from raw fish and has small eggs, about 30 µm, with a shouldered operculum.
whyNot.2: Schistosoma japonicum infects through the skin, and its eggs are non-operculated with a small lateral knob.
whyNot.3: Fasciolopsis buski is acquired from water plants such as water caltrop, and its eggs are larger, about 130–140 µm long.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., intestinal flukes; CDC DPDx, Echinostomiasis

items.stem: In a schistosomiasis survey in Leyte, a serologic test is done by incubating Schistosoma japonicum eggs with each resident's serum and then looking under the microscope for bleb-like or segmented precipitates attached to the egg shells. Which test is this?
items.why: **In the circumoval precipitin test (COPT), antibodies in the patient's serum react with antigens secreted by the miracidium inside the egg, forming precipitates around the egg shell.** The percentage of eggs with typical precipitates is reported, and the test has been widely used in Philippine schistosomiasis control alongside stool examination.

whyNot.0: Kato-Katz is a stool smear for counting eggs, not a serologic test.
whyNot.1: The miracidial hatching test places stool in water to watch for live miracidia; it does not use the patient's serum.
whyNot.2: The cercarienhüllen reaction looks for a membrane forming around cercariae, not eggs, in immune serum.

items.ref: Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed., blood flukes; Markell & Voge's Medical Parasitology, 10th ed.

items.stem: A mother brings in small, white, motile segments shaped like cucumber seeds that she found in her toddler's diaper. The family's dog has fleas. A crushed segment shows packets of eggs, each with several six-hooked embryos, and each segment has a genital pore on both sides. How did the child most likely become infected?
options: By accidentally swallowing an infected flea
By swallowing eggs passed in the dog's feces
By skin penetration of larvae in contaminated soil
items.why: Dipylidium caninum, the double-pored dog tapeworm, uses fleas as intermediate hosts. **Children are infected by swallowing fleas that carry the cysticercoid larva**, often while playing with pets. Motile, seed-shaped proglottids with two genital pores and egg packets are diagnostic.

whyNot.0: Undercooked pork transmits Taenia solium, whose proglottids have a single lateral genital pore and release single eggs.
whyNot.2: Swallowing eggs from dog feces transmits Echinococcus granulosus and Toxocara canis, not Dipylidium.
whyNot.3: Skin penetration is the route of hookworm and Strongyloides larvae, not of tapeworms.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Dipylidium caninum; Markell & Voge's Medical Parasitology, 10th ed., cestodes chapter

items.stem: Two days after swimming in a warm, poorly chlorinated freshwater pool, a teenager develops severe headache, fever and rapidly worsening confusion. A fresh, unrefrigerated CSF wet mount shows actively moving amoebae with blunt pseudopods. When placed in distilled water, some develop two flagella. Which organism is it?
items.why: Naegleria fowleri enters through the nose during swimming or diving in warm fresh water and causes rapidly fatal primary amebic meningoencephalitis. **Its ability to change into a flagellated form in distilled water distinguishes it from Acanthamoeba and Balamuthia.** CSF is examined fresh and never refrigerated so that the motile trophozoites can be seen.

whyNot.1: Balamuthia causes a slowly progressive granulomatous encephalitis and has no flagellate stage.
whyNot.2: Acanthamoeba causes subacute granulomatous amebic encephalitis or keratitis and has no flagellate stage.
whyNot.3: E. histolytica can reach the brain by spread from the liver, but it is not acquired by swimming and does not form flagellates.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Free-living amebic infections; Markell & Voge's Medical Parasitology, 10th ed.

items.stem: A forest worker from southern Palawan has daily fever spikes. His thin film shows normal-sized red cells containing ring forms, band-shaped trophozoites and rosette-like schizonts, with no Schüffner's dots, and the parasite density is very high. What should the laboratory do?
options: Report a mixed P. vivax and P. falciparum infection
Suspect Plasmodium knowlesi and confirm the species by PCR
Report Plasmodium malariae, because band forms are specific for it
Report Plasmodium ovale, because the red cells are not enlarged
items.why: Plasmodium knowlesi, a monkey malaria parasite transmitted in forested parts of Southeast Asia including Palawan, looks like P. malariae in its later stages and like P. falciparum in early rings. **A 24-hour cycle and a high parasite density with P. malariae-like morphology should raise suspicion of P. knowlesi, which is confirmed by PCR because microscopy cannot reliably identify it.** It can become severe quickly, so it is managed as a potentially severe infection.

whyNot.0: P. vivax enlarges red cells and shows Schüffner's dots, which are absent here, and band forms are not features of P. falciparum.
whyNot.2: Band forms are typical of but not specific for P. malariae, which has a 72-hour cycle and usually a low parasite density.
whyNot.3: P. ovale enlarges and ovalizes red cells and shows Schüffner's dots.

items.ref: WHO, Basic Malaria Microscopy, 2nd ed.; CDC DPDx, Malaria; Belizario & de Leon, Medical Parasitology in the Philippines, 3rd ed.

items.stem: On a Giemsa-stained thick blood film, 150 asexual Plasmodium falciparum parasites are counted against 200 white blood cells. The patient's measured WBC count is 6,000/µL. What is the parasite density?
items.why: Parasite density from a thick film is (parasites counted ÷ WBCs counted) × WBC count per µL. **150 ÷ 200 × 6,000 = 4,500 parasites/µL.** When no WBC count is available, an assumed value of 8,000/µL is used, but the patient's measured count is preferred.

whyNot.0: This divides by 400 WBCs instead of the 200 actually counted.
whyNot.2: This uses the assumed WBC count of 8,000/µL instead of the patient's measured count.
whyNot.3: This is ten times the correct value, a decimal error.

items.ref: WHO, Basic Malaria Microscopy, 2nd ed.; WHO, Malaria Parasite Counting, Malaria Microscopy SOP MM-SOP-09

worked.problem: On a thick film, 96 asexual malaria parasites are counted against 200 WBCs, and the patient's WBC count is 9,000/µL. Find the parasite density.

items.stem: An iodine-stained stool concentrate shows irregularly oval cysts about 8–10 µm long, each with a single nucleus and one large, sharply outlined vacuole that stains dark brown. Which organism is it?
items.why: Iodamoeba bütschlii cysts are small, usually uninucleate, and contain a large, well-defined glycogen vacuole. **The glycogen vacuole stains dark brown with iodine, which gives the organism its name.** It is a nonpathogen, but its presence shows ingestion of fecally contaminated food or water.

whyNot.0: Entamoeba hartmanni cysts have up to four nuclei with Entamoeba-type chromatin and may contain chromatoid bodies.
whyNot.1: Giardia cysts are oval with two to four nuclei, axonemes and median bodies, not a single large vacuole.
whyNot.3: Endolimax nana cysts are small and usually have four nuclei with large karyosomes, without a large glycogen vacuole.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Intestinal amebae (nonpathogenic); Markell & Voge's Medical Parasitology, 10th ed.

items.stem: A slide carries both a thick and a thin blood film for malaria diagnosis. Before Giemsa staining, only the thin film is dipped in methanol. Why is the thick film left unfixed?
options: So its red cells lyse in the water-based stain, leaving parasites visible
So the thick film dries faster before staining
Because methanol would stop Giemsa from staining parasite chromatin
Because the thick film is heat-fixed over a flame instead
items.why: The thick film contains several layers of red cells, which would hide the parasites if left intact. **Leaving it unfixed lets the red cells lyse (dehemoglobinize) in the aqueous Giemsa stain, so parasites and white cells stand out on a clear background.** The thin film is fixed with methanol so that its red cells stay intact for species identification.

whyNot.1: Fixation has nothing to do with drying; thick films are air-dried thoroughly before staining.
whyNot.2: Methanol-fixed thin films stain well with Giemsa, so methanol does not block chromatin staining.
whyNot.3: Malaria films are never heat-fixed, as heat fixes the hemoglobin and distorts the parasites.

items.ref: WHO, Basic Malaria Microscopy, 2nd ed.; CDC DPDx, Blood specimens: staining

items.stem: After centrifugation in the formalin–ethyl acetate concentration procedure, four layers form in the tube. Which portion is used to prepare the wet mount for ova and parasite examination?
options: The sediment at the bottom of the tube
The ethyl acetate layer at the top
The formalin layer above the sediment
items.why: Ethyl acetate extracts fat and debris, which collect as a plug between the solvent and the formalin. **Parasites, being denser, are packed in the sediment at the bottom, which is used for the wet mount after the upper layers are discarded.**

whyNot.1: The debris plug is rimmed free and poured off with the top layers.
whyNot.2: The ethyl acetate layer holds dissolved fats and is discarded.
whyNot.3: The formalin layer is discarded; the parasites have settled below it.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Stool specimens: specimen processing; Markell & Voge's Medical Parasitology, 10th ed., diagnostic methods

items.stem: An outpatient had a barium swallow X-ray study two days ago. Her physician now orders a stool ova and parasite examination. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Collect now, because barium does not interfere with microscopy
Postpone collection until the barium has cleared, about 7–10 days
Collect now and add extra formalin to dissolve the barium
Collect now and examine only a permanent stained smear
items.why: Barium crystals obscure parasites in wet mounts and stained smears and also reduce the number of organisms detected. **Stool collection should be delayed until the barium has cleared, usually about 7–10 days.** Mineral oil, bismuth, antidiarrheal agents and antibiotics can interfere in a similar way.

whyNot.0: Barium particles hide parasites and make the examination unreliable.
whyNot.2: Formalin preserves parasites but does not dissolve barium.
whyNot.3: Barium interferes with permanent stained smears as well as with wet mounts.

items.ref: CDC DPDx, Stool specimens: specimen collection; Markell & Voge's Medical Parasitology, 10th ed., diagnostic methods

items.stem: A laboratory uses the modified acid-fast (Kinyoun) stain to detect Cryptosporidium in stool. Which quality control practice is appropriate?
options: Stain a Giardia-positive smear once a month
Stain a negative fecal smear once a week
Stain a Cryptosporidium-positive smear with each run
Use no control if the background counterstain looks even
items.why: Stain performance can vary with reagent age, decolorizer strength and timing. **A control smear containing Cryptosporidium oocysts is stained each time patient smears are stained, and patient results are reported only if the oocysts stain the expected pink-red.** Control material can be prepared from preserved positive specimens.

whyNot.0: Giardia is not acid-fast, so it cannot show whether the acid-fast step worked, and monthly checks are too infrequent.
whyNot.1: A negative smear cannot show that oocysts will stain correctly.
whyNot.3: An even counterstain does not prove that the primary stain and decolorizer worked.

items.ref: CLSI M28, Procedures for the Recovery and Identification of Parasites From the Intestinal Tract; CDC DPDx, Stool specimens: staining procedures

items.stem: In a national malaria microscopy quality assurance program, each health facility sends a set of its routine slides to a reference laboratory for rechecking. Which approach best measures the accuracy of the facility's microscopists?
options: Rereading only slides with a high parasite density
Blinded rereading of a mix of positive and negative slides
Having each microscopist reread his or her own slides
Rereading only the slides the facility reported as positive
items.why: Rechecking should detect both false positives and false negatives. **Blinded rereading by validated microscopists of slides selected to include negatives as well as positives shows the facility's true error rates.** Feedback from rechecking is then used for retraining and supervision.

whyNot.0: High-density slides are the easiest to read, so rechecking only these would overestimate accuracy.
whyNot.2: Self-rechecking is not independent and tends to repeat the same errors.
whyNot.3: Checking only positives detects false positives but misses false negatives, which are the more dangerous errors.

items.ref: WHO, Malaria Microscopy Quality Assurance Manual, version 2 (2016)
